facts.hook: A diary found in 2013 logs the limestone shipped to the Great Pyramid
facts.body: The Diary of Merer, discovered at Wadi al-Jarf in 2013, documents the transport of white limestone blocks from Tura to the Great Pyramid.

facts.hook: Rebuilding Khufu's funeral boat took fourteen years
facts.body: It was found in 1954 buried in a pit beside the Great Pyramid. The ship was reassembled piece by piece over fourteen years.

facts.hook: The Great Pyramid's sarcophagus went in before the pyramid was finished
facts.body: The granite sarcophagus in the King's Chamber is too big to turn the corner between the passages, so it must have been set in place before the chamber's roof.

facts.hook: The Rosetta Stone looked black because of the wax that protected it
facts.body: In London it was covered in carnauba wax to protect it from visitors' fingers. The wax darkened the stone and it was mistaken for black basalt; a 1999 cleaning revealed its original dark grey.

facts.hook: The Rosetta Stone spent two years 15 metres underground in a postal railway station
facts.body: Towards the end of the First World War, in 1917, the museum moved it to safety from the bombing of London, to a station of the Postal Tube Railway.

facts.hook: An Egyptian decree called hieroglyphs the "language of the gods"
facts.body: The decree ordered a copy in every temple in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek, the language used by the Ptolemaic government.

facts.hook: Tutankhamun was one of the few pharaohs worshipped as a god while alive
facts.body: Temples for his cult were built as far away as Nubia, including one at Kawa and a smaller one at Faras.

facts.hook: Tutankhamun was first named "living image of Aten"
facts.body: He was born Tutankhaten, after the god Aten of his father Akhenaten. When traditional worship was restored, Aten gave way to Amun in his name.

facts.hook: According to Lucian, Sostratus hid his name under plaster on Alexandria's lighthouse
facts.body: In the second century AD, Lucian wrote that Sostratus hid his name under plaster bearing Ptolemy's name, so it would show in the stone once the plaster fell off.

facts.hook: Alexandria's harbour hid 30 sphinxes and 5 obelisks beside the lighthouse ruins
facts.body: In 1994 French archaeologists found remains of the lighthouse in the Eastern Harbour, including granite blocks of 49 to 60 tonnes.

facts.hook: Spanish, French and Italian words for lighthouse come from the island of Pharos
facts.body: The Alexandria lighthouse stood on the island of Pharos. Its name came to mean "lighthouse" in Greek and was borrowed by Romance languages such as Spanish, French and Italian.

facts.hook: A riot in Pompeii's amphitheatre in AD 59 led to a ten-year ban on events
facts.body: A serious riot and bloodshed broke out in the amphitheatre between Pompeians and Nucerians in AD 59. Further events there were banned for ten years.

facts.hook: Vesuvius may not have buried Pompeii in August: autumn fruit was found in the ruins
facts.body: It has long been dated to August, but several pieces of evidence point to October or November, such as the fresh fruit and vegetables in the shops, typical of October.

facts.hook: According to Dio Cassius, over 9,000 animals died at the Colosseum's inauguration
facts.body: Dio Cassius recounts that more than 9,000 wild animals were killed during the inaugural games of the amphitheatre.

facts.hook: The Colosseum is believed to owe its name to a colossal statue of Nero
facts.body: A giant bronze statue of Nero stood beside the amphitheatre, and the name Colosseum is believed to derive from it.

facts.hook: Seneca called garum an "expensive bloody mass of decayed fish"
facts.body: Seneca cautioned against this costly craze, even though his family was from Baetian Corduba. In his words, garum sociorum consumed the stomach with its salted putrefaction.

facts.hook: Roman fish sauce may have helped spread fish tapeworms across Europe
facts.body: This is a suggestion by the biological anthropologist Piers Mitchell about garum, the Roman fish sauce.

facts.hook: The Antikythera mechanism went unnoticed for two years in a museum
facts.body: Sponge divers found the wreck in early 1900. The mechanism looked like a lump of corroded bronze and wood until, in 1902, an archaeologist noticed a gear embedded in one piece.

facts.hook: The Antikythera mechanism timed six Greek games, not just eclipses
facts.body: Besides the calendar and solar eclipses, it tracked the timing of the panhellenic games: the four "crown" games, including Olympia, and two lesser ones.

facts.hook: Ancient Greek long jumpers swung weights in their hands
facts.body: In the long jump, competitors swung a pair of weights called halteres, often stones carved to fit the hand.

facts.hook: The ancient Olympics had a truce, and those who broke it were fined
facts.body: The truce was designed to let athletes and visitors travel safely to the games. Thucydides tells of violators who were fined 2,000 minae for attacking the city of Lepreum.

facts.hook: Hammurabi's Code: if a house collapsed and killed the homeowner, its builder was executed
facts.body: Law 229 states that the death of a homeowner in a house collapse necessitates the death of the house's builder.

facts.hook: Hammurabi's stele was found at Susa, where it had been taken as plunder
facts.body: It had been taken there as plunder. The French mission led by Jacques de Morgan dug it up in 1901, and it is now in the Louvre.

facts.hook: Cuneiform is thought to have grown out of accounting tokens kept in clay balls
facts.body: Clay tokens recorded amounts of livestock or goods. They were pressed onto round clay envelopes (bullae) and stored inside them, and were later replaced by flat tablets.

facts.hook: Machu Picchu's own fields could not feed the people who lived there
facts.body: Its terraces covered only about 4.9 hectares, too little to support more than 750 people. The food was probably imported from the surrounding valleys.

facts.hook: Inca quipus wrote zero as a gap: the absence of a knot
facts.body: On a quipu, clusters of knots on a cord represent digits in a base-10 system. A position with no knot stands for zero.

facts.hook: The shadow "serpent" on Chichen Itza's pyramid was probably not planned by the Maya
facts.body: Around the equinoxes, shadows make a serpent appear to wriggle down the staircase. But the effect lasts several weeks, so it cannot fix any date by itself.

facts.hook: Aztec shoppers paid small bills in cacao and big ones in cloth
facts.body: Small purchases were made with cacao beans. For larger purchases, standardized lengths of cotton cloth, called quachtli, were used.

facts.hook: The Mexica did not call themselves "Aztecs"
facts.body: "Aztec" was not used as a self-name by the Aztecs themselves. The modern use of the word dates from Alexander von Humboldt, in 1810.

facts.hook: The Maya measured Venus's 584-day cycle to within two hours
facts.body: Venus was closely tied to warfare: the Maya hieroglyph for "war" included the planet's symbol.

facts.hook: Columbus met a Maya canoe with 25 rowers, loaded with cacao and obsidian
facts.body: It was made from a hollowed-out tree trunk and was 2.5 metres broad. It carried cacao, obsidian, ceramics, textiles, and copper bells and axes.

facts.hook: The platypus hunts with its eyes, ears and nose shut
facts.body: Underwater it closes its eyes, ears and nose and digs along the stream bed with its bill. Electroreceptors in the bill detect the tiny electric currents made when its prey's muscles contract.

facts.hook: A hummingbird can slow its metabolism to 1/15 of normal
facts.body: When food is scarce or at night, hummingbirds enter torpor, a state like hibernation, and slow their metabolic rate to one fifteenth of its normal rate.

facts.hook: Hummingbird eggs are the smallest of any bird
facts.body: A hummingbird typically lays two pea-sized white eggs, which are incubated for two to three weeks.

facts.hook: Some male hummingbirds court by diving from 30 metres
facts.body: During courtship some species dive from 30 metres above a female at around 23 m/s, which is about 83 km/h.

facts.hook: Chameleons change colour more to show their state than to hide
facts.body: Colour change can help with camouflage, but it is used most commonly for social signalling and in reaction to temperature. It tells other chameleons about the animal's physical condition and intentions.

facts.hook: Chameleons move each eye on its own
facts.body: Each eye can pivot and focus independently, so a chameleon can watch two objects at once. When it hunts, the eyes focus forward together.

facts.hook: African bush elephants are pregnant for about 22 months, longer than any other mammal
facts.body: In African bush elephant cows, gestation lasts around 22 months, the longest of any mammal.

facts.hook: The blue whale's species name, musculus, can also mean "little mouse"
facts.body: Musculus could mean "muscle" or a diminutive form of "mouse", possibly a pun by Linnaeus when he named the species.

facts.hook: A blue whale calf gains about 90 kilos a day
facts.body: A newborn blue whale calf gains roughly 90 kilograms (200 lb) of weight every single day.

facts.hook: Drone honey bees have a mother but no father
facts.body: Drones are haploid: they have only one set of chromosomes and are descended only from their mother, the queen.

facts.hook: A bee larva becomes a queen because of what it eats
facts.body: Worker and queen larvae are both fed royal jelly for the first three days. Then future workers switch to pollen and nectar, while future queens keep getting royal jelly and grow into queens.

facts.hook: "Narwhal" means "corpse-whale" in Old Norse
facts.body: The word comes from the Old Norse nárhval, which possibly refers to the animal's grey, mottled skin.

facts.hook: Some male narwhals grow two tusks
facts.body: The usual tusk is a canine tooth that projects from the left side of the upper jaw. Some males also grow a second one, when the right canine protrudes through the lip too.

facts.hook: Young ravens slide down snowbanks just for fun
facts.body: Juvenile common ravens are among the most playful of all birds. They have been seen sliding down snowbanks, apparently purely for fun.

facts.hook: Ravens have been seen at 6,350 metres on Everest
facts.body: In Tibet, common ravens have been recorded at up to 5,000 m, and as high as 6,350 m on Mount Everest.

facts.hook: Two thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms
facts.body: The nerve cords of its arms hold two thirds of its neurons, which lets the arms perform actions with a degree of independence.

facts.hook: An octopus tastes what it touches with its suckers
facts.body: Its suction cups have chemoreceptors that let it taste what it touches. And sensors that recognise octopus skin stop the arms from sticking to themselves.

facts.hook: Even the largest octopus species can squeeze through a gap just over 2.5 cm wide
facts.body: Most of an octopus's body is soft tissue, so it can squeeze through tiny gaps.

facts.hook: The sperm whale has the biggest brain of any animal
facts.body: Even so, it is not that big for its body size: its encephalization quotient is lower than that of many other whales and dolphins.

facts.hook: The sperm whale makes the loudest sound of any animal
facts.body: It uses echolocation and vocal sounds louder than those of any other animal. When echolocating, it sends out a focused beam of clicks.

facts.hook: Seahorses have no real stomach, so they must eat constantly
facts.body: Their digestive system is extremely simple and lacks a stomach, so they have to eat constantly to stay alive.

facts.hook: In seahorses, the male carries the eggs in a pouch
facts.body: The female deposits her eggs in the male's brood pouch, and he carries them until the young are released into the water fully developed.

facts.hook: A naked mole-rat queen grows a longer backbone
facts.body: Once a new queen is established, her body widens the spaces between the vertebrae of her backbone, so she becomes longer and ready to bear pups.

facts.hook: The naked mole-rat is one of only two known eusocial mammals
facts.body: Its colony has separate breeding and non-breeding castes, and when the queen dies, another female takes her place, often after a violent struggle.

facts.hook: European eel larvae drift across the Atlantic for about 300 days
facts.body: The Sargasso Sea is their most likely spawning ground. From there the larvae drift all the way to the coasts of Europe.

facts.hook: A clam named Ming lived for 507 years
facts.body: This Arctica islandica clam was collected alive by an expedition in 2006, and its reported age was 507 years.

facts.hook: A cheetah goes from 0 to 97 km/h in under 3 seconds
facts.body: Its acceleration is exceptional: by comparison, polo horses take 3.6 seconds to go from 0 to 36 km/h.

facts.hook: Picasso and Apollinaire were both suspects in the Mona Lisa theft
facts.body: After the Louvre theft in 1911, poet Guillaume Apollinaire was arrested and named his friend Pablo Picasso, who was brought in for questioning. Both were later cleared.

facts.hook: The Mona Lisa thief got caught trying to sell it to the Uffizi
facts.body: Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian patriot who thought it belonged in an Italian museum, stole it from the Louvre in 1911. After about two years he grew impatient and offered it to the Uffizi's director.

facts.hook: The Prado holds a Mona Lisa painted at the same time as Leonardo's
facts.body: Restored in 2012, the Madrid copy is now thought to come from Leonardo's own studio, made while he was painting the original. The Prado says it is probably by Salaì or Melzi, two of his pupils.

facts.hook: Caravaggio painted straight onto the canvas, without preparatory drawings
facts.body: He worked fast from live models and skipped drawings. His dramatic use of light and dark came to be known as tenebrism.

facts.hook: Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights was once known as «Del Madroño»
facts.body: The title we use today is modern. The record of its transfer to El Escorial, dated 8 July 1593, describes a painting by Bosch with grotesqueries, known as «Del Madroño».
facts.src: Wikipedia · The Garden of Earthly Delights

facts.hook: Botero was expelled from school after writing an essay about Picasso
facts.body: As a young man, Botero worked as a newspaper illustrator to support his artistic interests. After he wrote an essay defending Picasso's art, he was expelled from school.

facts.hook: Duchamp's original urinal was lost, and a Stieglitz photo documents it
facts.body: After it was kept out of the show, Fountain was photographed at Alfred Stieglitz's studio, but the original has been lost. The replicas that exist were later commissioned from Duchamp.

facts.hook: Picasso wanted Guernica kept out of Spain until it had liberty and democracy
facts.body: At Picasso's request, New York's Museum of Modern Art took charge of the painting. He did not want it sent to Spain until liberty and democracy were established there. It stayed at MoMA until 1981.

facts.hook: A forger escaped a Nazi-collaborator charge by confessing his Vermeer was fake
facts.body: In 1945 Han van Meegeren was arrested as an alleged Nazi collaborator over a 'Vermeer' sold to Hermann Göring. He confessed he had painted it himself, and was convicted and sentenced to just one year in prison.

facts.hook: A Vermeer forger baked his paintings at 100 to 120 °C
facts.body: Han van Meegeren wanted his forgeries to look 300 years old. After finishing each one, he baked it to harden the paint and used a cylinder to increase the cracking.

facts.hook: Leonardo wrote the notes of his Vitruvian Man in mirror writing
facts.body: He based the drawing on Vitruvius but corrected inaccuracies in his account. The fragile drawing is kept in Venice and rarely displayed.

facts.hook: Some people were accused of smashing pottery on purpose to mend it with kintsugi
facts.body: Kintsugi mends broken pottery with lacquer dusted or mixed with powdered gold, silver or platinum. It became so prized that some were accused of breaking pottery on purpose so it could get the gold seams.

facts.hook: Hokusai rose to fame in 1804 with a 240-square-metre drawing of a monk
facts.body: He drew Daruma, a Buddhist monk, for a festival in Tokyo. Over his life he used more than 30 pseudonyms.
facts.src: Wikipedia · The Great Wave off Kanagawa

facts.hook: "If I haven't fought for my country, at least I'll paint for her", Delacroix wrote
facts.body: Delacroix wrote it to his brother in 1830, having embarked on a painting of a barricade: Liberty Leading the People. The French government bought the painting in 1831.

facts.hook: Van Gogh painted The Starry Night by day, in a studio at his asylum
facts.body: The view is from the east-facing window of his asylum room, but the picture was painted in daylight in a ground-floor studio. The village in it was not visible from his room.

facts.hook: The brightest star in The Starry Night is actually the planet Venus
facts.body: In spring 1889 Venus was visible at dawn in Provence and nearly as bright as possible. It is the bright point just right of the cypress tree.

facts.hook: Rembrandt's Night Watch is not a night scene: dark varnish made it look like one
facts.body: For much of its life the painting was coated with dark varnish, which gave the false impression of a night scene and the name we use today. The varnish was only removed in the 1940s.

facts.hook: The sitters in The Night Watch paid to appear in it: about a hundred guilders each
facts.body: In total, Rembrandt was paid 1,600 guilders for the painting, a large sum at the time.

facts.hook: Kahlo painted The Two Fridas the year she divorced Rivera, then remarried him
facts.body: Frida Kahlo painted this double self-portrait in 1939, the year of her divorce from Diego Rivera. They remarried a year later.

facts.hook: Guayasamin did not live to see his Chapel of Man finished
facts.body: The Ecuadorian painter died in 1999. The building he co-designed in Quito was completed and opened to the public in 2002.

facts.hook: Goya painted his Black Paintings straight onto the walls of his own house
facts.body: The 14 works were painted as murals in the Quinta del Sordo. Transferring them to canvas was a slow process that began in 1874, and they are now in the Prado.

facts.hook: One panel of the Ghent Altarpiece is a copy: the original was stolen in 1934
facts.body: It is The Just Judges panel. The Belgian restorer Jef Van der Veken produced the copy, and the original has never been recovered.

facts.hook: A suffragette attacked Velázquez's Rokeby Venus with a meat cleaver in 1914
facts.body: Mary Richardson left seven slashes on the canvas, all of which were successfully repaired. She was sentenced to six months in prison, the maximum allowed for destroying an artwork.

facts.hook: Las Meninas wasn't called that until 1843, when a Prado catalogue named it
facts.body: Early inventories called it The Family, later The Family of Philip IV. The Prado catalogue of 1843 listed it for the first time as Las Meninas.

facts.hook: Las Meninas is the only Velázquez painting that shows a ceiling
facts.body: The room is the painter's most thoroughly rendered architectural space.

facts.hook: Leonardo's Last Supper began to deteriorate soon after it was finished
facts.body: Leonardo skipped fresco, which does not let a painter work slowly, and tried another method. Because of the method used, the painting began to deteriorate soon after it was completed.

facts.hook: Artemisia Gentileschi was the first woman admitted to Florence's art academy
facts.body: The painter became a member of the Accademia di Arte del Disegno in Florence and had an international clientele.

facts.hook: The Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry but an embroidery nearly 70 metres long
facts.body: Its images are stitched rather than woven into the cloth. It is about 50 centimetres tall.

facts.hook: The Bayeux Tapestry narrowly escaped being used to cover military wagons
facts.body: During the French Revolution, in 1792, it was confiscated as public property to cover military wagons, and it narrowly escaped destruction.

facts.hook: Remedios Varo went into exile in Mexico but never became Mexican
facts.body: She arrived in 1941, after the Nazis reached Paris, and never returned to Spain. Despite widespread belief, she kept her Spanish citizenship, unlike her friend Leonora Carrington.

facts.hook: A bear was drafted into the Polish army so it could board a ship
facts.body: The British transport to Italy forbade mascots and pets. To get around it, Wojtek, a brown bear travelling with Polish soldiers, was officially drafted into the Polish Army as a private.

facts.hook: A bear carrying a shell became the official emblem of a Polish unit
facts.body: Wojtek, a bear who served with a Polish artillery supply company, was so popular that a picture of a bear carrying an artillery shell became the unit's official emblem.

facts.hook: In 1518, Strasbourg tried to cure a dancing plague with more dancing
facts.body: It began in July 1518, when a woman known as Frau Troffea started dancing in a street. The council handed authority to physicians, who prescribed that the afflicted dance themselves free of it.

facts.hook: In 1666, gunpowder was used to make firebreaks against the Great Fire of London
facts.body: It broke out shortly after midnight on 2 September 1666 at Thomas Farriner's bakery. It is thought to have been beaten by two factors: the east wind dropped, and the Tower of London garrison used gunpowder to make firebreaks.

facts.hook: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years, but that name came later
facts.body: Historians date the war to 116 years, though it was intermittent, with interruptions like the Black Death and truces. The name "Hundred Years' War" was adopted by later historians.

facts.hook: A captain's ear, allegedly cut off, helped push Britain into war with Spain
facts.body: British captain Robert Jenkins said a Spanish coast guard captain severed his ear in 1731. In 1738, opposition politicians used the incident to push for war against Spain, which was fought from 1739.

facts.hook: In 1741, a British fleet of 186 ships failed to take Cartagena de Indias
facts.body: The fleet had 186 ships, 60 more than Philip II's famous Spanish Armada. Cartagena's strong fortifications and Spanish commander Blas de Lezo's strategy repelled it, in the war's most significant operation.

facts.hook: Onoda kept fighting in the Philippines until 1974, when his old commander told him to stop
facts.body: He took the leaflets announcing the war's end for Allied propaganda. In 1974, his former commanding officer, Major Yoshimi Taniguchi, flew to the island to relieve him of duty.

facts.hook: Norio Suzuki set out to find Onoda, a panda and the abominable snowman, in that order
facts.body: Norio Suzuki, a Japanese adventurer travelling the world, found Onoda on Lubang on 20 February 1974. Onoda still refused to surrender until his former commander relieved him of duty.

facts.hook: After a failed rice-cornering gamble, a man declared himself US emperor in 1859
facts.body: Joshua Norton's failed attempt to corner the rice market led to a lost court case and bankruptcy. On September 17, 1859, he hand-delivered a letter to a San Francisco newspaper declaring himself "Emperor of these United States".

facts.hook: After the Bounty mutiny, Bligh sailed more than 6,500 km in an open launch
facts.body: On 28 April 1789, mutineers set Captain Bligh and 18 loyalists adrift in the ship's open launch with about five days' food and water. They navigated more than 6,500 km to reach safety.

facts.hook: The Bounty's captain's cabin became a greenhouse for over 1,000 breadfruit plants
facts.body: The ship was fitted out to carry breadfruit from Tahiti to the West Indies. Its great cabin got glazed windows, skylights and a drainage system to avoid wasting fresh water.

facts.hook: Nellie Bly circled the globe in 72 days and met Jules Verne on the way
facts.body: She set off on November 14, 1889, to turn Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days into fact, and was back in New York on January 25, 1890, just over 72 days later. In Amiens, she met Verne himself.

facts.hook: Nellie Bly got herself committed to a New York asylum to expose abuses from inside
facts.body: Working for Pulitzer's New York World, she feigned insanity to investigate brutality and neglect at the Women's Lunatic Asylum on Blackwell's Island. Once committed, she saw the deplorable conditions firsthand.

facts.hook: A corpse with fake papers dumped off Huelva fooled the Germans
facts.body: In April 1943 the British dressed a body as a Royal Marines officer and put fake documents on it; it was found near Huelva, Spain. German reinforcements went to Greece and Sardinia, and none to Sicily.

facts.hook: The Mincemeat corpse was given a fictional fiancée named Pam
facts.body: To make the fake officer believable, the British gave him an invented fiancée, Pam, with a photo of an MI5 clerk and love letters. His identity was William Martin of the Royal Marines.

facts.hook: The Pastry War between France and Mexico was named after one man's complaint
facts.body: French pastry chef Remontel said Mexican officers looted his shop in Tacubaya in 1832; Mexican sources said they simply refused to pay their bills. His complaint, among others from French nationals, gave the war its name.

facts.hook: The Treaty of Tordesillas never said which Cape Verde island its line was measured from
facts.body: Signed in 1494, it split newly found lands between Portugal and Castile along a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. It didn't define the league in degrees or the starting island, and the joint voyage meant to settle that never happened.

facts.hook: At Christmas 1914, around 100,000 British and German soldiers stopped fighting
facts.body: The Germans placed candles on their trenches and Christmas trees and sang carols, and the British answered with their own. Then men crossed no man's land to swap food, tobacco and small gifts.

facts.hook: The pope asked for a Christmas truce in 1914; governments refused, soldiers made one
facts.body: On 7 December 1914, Pope Benedict XV asked that the guns fall silent at least on the night the angels sang, but both sides refused. Soldiers still arranged unofficial ceasefires.

facts.hook: In 1810, pirate leader Zheng Yi Sao negotiated her surrender and avoided prosecution
facts.body: She led a pirate confederation in the South China Sea. In 1810 she surrendered to the Qing with 24 ships and over 1,400 pirates, avoided prosecution, and died in 1844 after a relatively peaceful life.

facts.hook: A Chinese pirate confederation in 1805 had six fleets, one per flag color
facts.body: Zheng Yi united the pirates through an agreement signed in July 1805. He fell overboard in a gale in 1807, and his widow, Zheng Yi Sao, inherited his informal command of the confederation.

facts.hook: A man unable to form new memories still learned to draw with a mirror
facts.body: Henry Molaison could not form new long-term memories, yet in the early 1960s he learned to draw a figure by looking at it in a mirror, improving with each attempt without remembering any of them.

facts.hook: Unable to make new memories, a man drew a detailed map of his new home
facts.body: Five years after his surgery Henry Molaison moved house, and despite his amnesia he could still draw a fairly detailed map of it. One hypothesis is that he built it by walking through it every day.

facts.hook: Reading is so automatic that naming an ink color gets harder if the word says another
facts.body: If "red" is printed in blue ink, you take longer and make more mistakes naming the ink. It is explained by the automation of reading: the mind gets the word's meaning automatically.

facts.hook: The McGurk effect was discovered by accident in a study of how infants perceive language
facts.body: A technician dubbed a video with a different phoneme from the one spoken. When it was played back, both researchers heard a third phoneme, neither of the two.

facts.hook: Knowing how the McGurk illusion works does not make it go away
facts.body: Some optical illusions break down once you "see through" them, but this one does not. Researchers who have studied it for more than twenty years still experience it.

facts.hook: People who score worst on a test tend to think they placed in the top half
facts.body: Compared with others, the bottom quartile tends to see itself in the top two quartiles. This is the Dunning-Kruger effect, first studied with logical reasoning, grammar and social skills.

facts.hook: The Ponzo illusion also fools touch, but not people blind from birth
facts.body: Two identical lines drawn across converging lines look different, and the effect also occurs in touch. But prior visual experience seems necessary: people blind from birth are not sensitive to it.

facts.hook: Ebbinghaus tested his own memory with nonsense syllables like "WID" and "ZOF"
facts.body: Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a study on himself, testing his memory after various intervals, and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis.

facts.hook: A waiter remembered unpaid orders but forgot the ones already settled
facts.body: This is how the Zeigarnik effect began: Kurt Lewin noticed a waiter remembered unpaid orders better. Once everyone had paid, he could no longer recall any more details of them.

facts.hook: Raising your voice in noise is an involuntary tendency also found in birds and monkeys
facts.body: Étienne Lombard discovered in 1909 the involuntary tendency to speak louder in noise. Research on birds and monkeys finds the effect also occurs in animal vocalizations.

facts.hook: Your brain reacts to a face in an object in 165 ms, almost as fast as to a real face
facts.body: A 2009 study measured activation of the brain's face area: a face-like object triggers it at 165 ms, only slightly later than a real face (130 ms). So it is not a late reinterpretation.

facts.hook: Invisible gorilla test: in most groups, half did not report seeing the gorilla
facts.body: Subjects count passes in a video while a person in a gorilla suit walks through the scene. In most groups, 50% did not report seeing the gorilla.

facts.hook: People walking on the phone are the least likely to notice a clown on a unicycle
facts.body: An experiment compared walkers talking on the phone, listening to a digital audio player, or walking alone or in pairs. Those on a phone call were least likely to notice the clown.

facts.hook: An iron rod went through his skull, and Gage told the doctor: "here is business enough"
facts.body: In 1848 a large iron rod was driven completely through Phineas Gage's head in a blasting accident. A doctor found him sitting in a chair outside the hotel, and Gage said: "Doctor, here is business enough for you."

facts.hook: People who can't recognize faces often rely on clothing, gait or voice
facts.body: People with prosopagnosia often learn other strategies, paying more attention to secondary clues to tell who is who.

facts.hook: Some patients who can't recognize faces still react to familiar ones through their skin
facts.body: In 1984 Bauer found that patients with prosopagnosia, unable to recognize faces consciously, still showed automatic arousal, measured through the skin, to familiar faces. It suggests two pathways: conscious and unconscious.

facts.hook: Your brain uses as much energy in REM sleep as when awake, or more
facts.body: In REM sleep, the brain's use of oxygen and glucose equals or exceeds that of waking. In non-REM sleep the rate is 11 to 40% lower.

facts.hook: In alien hand syndrome, a hand can unbutton a blouse without its owner's control
facts.body: In this condition, a limb seems to act on its own, without conscious control. One patient buttoned her blouse with one hand while the other unbuttoned it. The first known case was published in 1908 by Kurt Goldstein.

facts.hook: British children gained 14 IQ points on the Raven test between 1942 and 2008
facts.body: This is the Flynn effect: similar gains have been seen in other countries with long, widespread IQ testing, including other Western European countries, Japan and South Korea.

facts.hook: Darth Vader never says "Luke, I am your father": he says "No, I am your father"
facts.body: It is an example of the Mandela effect, a false memory shared by many people. In The Empire Strikes Back, the line does not include Luke's name.

facts.hook: 39 students rated an identical personality vignette 4.30 out of 5 for accuracy
facts.body: Forer gave his students a supposedly personal vignette, but it was identical for all and came from an astrology book. They still rated it as highly accurate.

facts.hook: In 1867 a French sinologist published a book on how to direct your dreams
facts.body: The Marquis d'Hervey de Saint Denys published it anonymously: Dreams and the ways to direct them. In it he proposed that it is possible to learn to dream consciously, that is, knowing you are dreaming.

facts.hook: Sleepwalkers usually get up in the first third of the night, in slow-wave sleep
facts.body: Sleepwalking happens in slow-wave sleep, and episodes typically occur in the first third of the night, when that stage is most prominent.

facts.hook: The halo effect was shown in 1920 by having officers rate their soldiers
facts.body: Edward Thorndike asked commanding officers to rate their soldiers. Ratings tended to treat each person as rather good or rather inferior across all qualities.

facts.hook: Once we know an outcome, we often believe we knew it all along
facts.body: Hindsight bias can distort the memory of what we knew or believed before an event, making us feel we could have predicted it.

facts.hook: Two equal lines look different depending on which way their arrow fins point
facts.body: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, devised in 1889, equal segments look longer or shorter depending on whether the fins point inwards or outwards.

facts.hook: In sleep paralysis you are conscious, but your body seems to stay in REM sleep
facts.body: It is a state, on waking or falling asleep, in which a person is conscious but paralyzed. One explanation is an overlap of REM and waking stages, so REM features persist after waking.

facts.hook: The Barnum effect is named after a showman, not after the psychologist who described it
facts.body: Forer called it the "fallacy of personal validation". In 1956 Paul Meehl coined "Barnum effect", comparing vague test descriptions to those of showman P. T. Barnum.

facts.hook: The sensitive plant folds its leaves inward when you touch it
facts.body: When touched or shaken, the compound leaves of Mimosa pudica quickly fold inward and droop, then re-open a few minutes later.

facts.hook: The Venus flytrap can tell live prey from a falling raindrop
facts.body: Its trap only fully closes if two trigger hairs are touched within 20 seconds, or one hair twice in quick succession. The lobes then snap shut in about a tenth of a second.

facts.hook: Small prey can slip out through gaps in a Venus flytrap's trap
facts.body: Presumably the benefit from them would be less than the cost of digesting them. If they escape, the trap usually reopens within 12 hours.

facts.hook: According to Darwin, a gnat's leg on one tentacle is enough to make a sundew react
facts.body: All sundew species can move their tentacles when they touch edible prey. Drosera capensis can curl its leaf completely around the prey in 30 minutes.

facts.hook: Aquatic bladderworts can catch tadpoles with suction traps
facts.body: Their traps are bladders that suck prey in. In aquatic species such as U. vulgaris the bladders are usually larger and can catch prey from mosquito larvae to young tadpoles.

facts.hook: The rootless waterwheel plant snaps its trap shut in 10 to 20 milliseconds
facts.body: Aldrovanda is a rootless aquatic plant. Its trap closes in 10 to 20 milliseconds, one of the fastest plant movements.

facts.hook: The largest single flower on Earth belongs to a plant with no leaves or roots
facts.body: The Rafflesia arnoldii flower grows to around 1 m across and weighs up to 11 kg, while the plant itself lacks any observable leaves, stems or roots.

facts.hook: The talipot palm flowers only once in its life, then dies
facts.body: It flowers between the ages of 30 and 80 and dies after fruiting. Its inflorescence, 6 to 8 m long, is the largest of any plant.

facts.hook: Scientists regenerated a plant from frozen remains about 32,000 years old
facts.body: In 2012, a team of Russian scientists regenerated Silene stenophylla from frozen samples that radiocarbon dating put at around 32,000 years old.

facts.hook: Welwitschia has just two leaves, and they never stop growing
facts.body: This plant of the Namib desert has a large woody stem with only two leaves that grow throughout its life. It is native to Angola and Namibia.

facts.hook: Some bristlecone pine needles stay green for 45 years
facts.body: The leaves of this pine are among the longest-lasting of any plant, and some remain green for 45 years.

facts.hook: Posidonia, a Mediterranean seagrass, has floating fruits called sea olives
facts.body: Posidonia is a seagrass with roots, rhizomes and ribbon-shaped leaves. Its fruit floats freely and is known in Italy as the olive of the sea.

facts.hook: What looks like a ginkgo fruit is not a fruit but a seed
facts.body: Ginkgo is a gymnosperm, and its apricot-like "fruits" are really seeds. Their soft, fleshy outer layer contains butyric acid and smells like rancid butter.

facts.hook: A dodder seedling with no host to attach to dies within 10 days at most
facts.body: If a dodder seedling has not reached a plant within 5 to 10 days of germination, it dies.

facts.hook: The giant Amazon water lily traps beetles in its flower, and they leave covered in pollen
facts.body: The petals start out white and turn reddish pink while the beetles are inside. Once out, the beetles carry the pollen to other newly opened water lilies.

facts.hook: A giant water lily inspired Paxton's Crystal Palace
facts.body: Joseph Paxton took inspiration from the lily's ribbed undersurface for the Crystal Palace, a building four times the size of St. Peter's in Rome.

facts.hook: Sandbox tree fruits explode and can fling their seeds at 70 m/s
facts.body: When ripe, the capsules of Hura crepitans explode and launch seeds at 70 m/s (250 km/h). That is why it is nicknamed the "dynamite tree".

facts.hook: Spanish moss is not a moss but a rootless bromeliad
facts.body: It often grows on large trees, but it is not a parasite: it absorbs water and nutrients from the air and rain through its own leaves.

facts.hook: One bamboo species has been recorded flowering only once every 120 years
facts.body: In that species, all plants of the same stock flower at the same time, wherever they grow, which points to some sort of "alarm clock" in each cell.

facts.hook: The Moreton Bay fig often starts life on another tree and ends up strangling it
facts.body: Its seed usually germinates in the canopy of a host tree. When its roots reach the ground, it enlarges, strangles the host and ends up a freestanding tree.

facts.hook: Figs are pollinated only by fig wasps, which can breed only in fig flowers
facts.body: It is an obligate mutualism: neither side can do without the other.

facts.hook: Wild Wollemi pines are all genetically indistinguishable
facts.body: They were discovered in 1994. This suggests their population once fell so low, possibly to one or two individuals, that all genetic variability was lost.

facts.hook: With only 23 people, a shared birthday is more likely than not
facts.body: The chance that at least two share a birthday exceeds 50%, because every possible pair is compared. For someone to match YOUR birthday with over 50% odds, you need at least 253 people.

facts.hook: A 1927 experiment with solid-looking pitch drips about once a decade
facts.body: Thomas Parnell started it in Australia to show students that some substances that appear solid are highly viscous fluids. Each drop takes about a decade to form and fall.

facts.hook: Very cold helium can lose all its viscosity and flow without friction
facts.body: A superfluid has zero viscosity: when stirred, it forms vortices that keep rotating indefinitely. It happens in two isotopes of helium when they are cooled to cryogenic temperatures.

facts.hook: You can walk on a tub of cornstarch and water without sinking, if you step fast
facts.body: It is a non-Newtonian fluid: with slow motions it is a fairly viscous liquid, but a sudden impact briefly turns it into a near solid mass. After the blow, it goes back to being liquid.

facts.hook: Break sugar in the dark and it gives off tiny flashes, as Francis Bacon noted in 1620
facts.body: It is called triboluminescence: light given off when a material is crushed, scratched or pulled apart. It is not fully understood, but in most cases it seems to come from electric charges separating and reuniting.

facts.hook: Sound can make a liquid emit light: it was found in 1934 during sonar work
facts.body: At the University of Cologne, Frenzel and Schultes, working on sonar, noticed that bubbles in a liquid gave off light when ultrasound was on. It is called sonoluminescence.

facts.hook: Hitchcock paid for Psycho himself because Paramount didn't want him to make it
facts.body: The studio called the novel "impossible for films". Hitchcock made it through his own company and took a 60% stake in the negative instead of his usual $250,000 fee.

facts.hook: Norman Bates's house was modeled on an Edward Hopper painting
facts.body: The mansion in Psycho copies the Victorian house in Hopper's "House by the Railroad". It was built on the same stage where The Phantom of the Opera was filmed in 1925.

facts.hook: Hitchcock hid fake corpses of "Mrs. Bates" in his star's dressing room
facts.body: During filming he made several versions of the "Mother corpse" prop and left them in Janet Leigh's closet. She took the joke well and wondered if it was meant to keep her in suspense or to judge which corpse would scare audiences more.

facts.hook: Jaws was scheduled to shoot for 55 days and took 159
facts.body: Shooting at sea brought constant trouble, and the mechanical sharks often malfunctioned. It wrapped on October 6, 1974. Spielberg later said he thought his career as a filmmaker was over.

facts.hook: A real great white attacked an empty cage and changed the script of Jaws
facts.body: The Taylors filmed real sharks off Australia. When a great white attacked the empty cage, Spielberg wanted the footage, so the script had Hooper escape from the cage first.

facts.hook: Jaws avoided the color red so that only the blood would be red
facts.body: Spielberg asked the art department to keep red out of the sets and costumes. That way the blood from the attacks was the only red on screen and hit harder.

facts.hook: A copy of Metropolis's original cut turned up in Buenos Aires in 2008
facts.body: A damaged print of Fritz Lang's original cut was found in a museum in Argentina. Together with a second print archived in New Zealand, it allowed a restoration shown in Berlin and Frankfurt in 2010.

facts.hook: Metropolis (1927) faked its city with miniatures and mirror tricks
facts.body: Effects expert Eugen Schüfftan used miniatures of the city and his Schüfftan process, in which mirrors create the illusion that actors are inside miniature sets.

facts.hook: Metropolis was the first film on UNESCO's Memory of the World register
facts.body: This 1927 German silent film was inscribed on the register in 2001, the first film to receive that distinction.

facts.hook: King Kong's dinosaurs were built for another film that was never finished
facts.body: Effects creator Willis O'Brien reused the dinosaur models from his own aborted film project, Creation. King Kong's production was completed in January 1933.

facts.hook: The Tin Man's joint oil in The Wizard of Oz was chocolate syrup
facts.body: The Tin Man's costume was leather-covered buckram, and the oil used to grease his joints was made from chocolate syrup. The Lion's costume used real lion skin and fur.

facts.hook: The Wizard of Oz's tornado was a stretch of muslin hung from a crane
facts.body: After a rubber version failed, the crew hung 11 metres of muslin from a steel gantry and sprayed fuller's earth with air hoses. The footage was later recycled in a 1943 film.

facts.hook: The Wizard of Oz made no profit until its 1949 re-release
facts.body: It was MGM's most expensive production at the time and failed to make a profit until 1949. A 1956 CBS television broadcast then reintroduced it to the public.

facts.hook: The Scarecrow's mask left permanent lines on Ray Bolger's face
facts.body: The masks were made of foam latex, a technique makeup artist Jack Dawn was among the first to use. Peeling Bolger's mask off took an hour a day and eventually left permanent lines around his mouth and chin.

facts.hook: Gene Kelly danced in the rain with a 39 °C fever, and not in one take
facts.body: A common myth says Kelly filmed the whole song in a single take, but the sequence took two to three days. He was also sick with a fever at the time.

facts.hook: Singin' in the Rain (1952) was built around songs from 1929-39 MGM films
facts.body: Producer Arthur Freed wanted a film for his catalog of songs written with Nacio Herb Brown. Since many were written as silent films gave way to talkies, the story was set in that transition.

facts.hook: Hitchcock cut the conventional music from The Birds and played with silence
facts.body: He did without a conventional incidental score, using sound effects, sparse source music and calculated silences. Most birds were real, though an estimated $200,000+ went on mechanical ones.

facts.hook: The broken mirror in Apocalypse Now was real, and so was Martin Sheen's blood
facts.body: In the opening scene Sheen punched a mirror that was not a prop, and it made his hand bleed heavily. He insisted on continuing the scene despite Coppola's concerns.

facts.hook: Martin Sheen's brother Joe stood in for him on Apocalypse Now after a heart attack
facts.body: Sheen had a heart attack during filming. Until he returned to the set, his brother Joe Estevez filled in, shot from behind so Martin's close-ups could be filmed once he recovered.

facts.hook: Los santos inocentes was the highest-grossing Spanish film in Spain at the time
facts.body: Directed by Mario Camus and released in 1984, it was a box-office hit. At Cannes, Francisco Rabal and Alfredo Landa shared the Best Actor Award.

facts.hook: Berlanga had to feature singer Lolita Sevilla in Welcome Mr. Marshall!
facts.body: He was commissioned to make a vehicle for the budding flamenco singer, but chose to give the film a deeper, more satirical meaning.

facts.hook: Casablanca was based on a play that had never been staged
facts.body: Producer Hal Wallis bought the rights to Everybody Comes to Rick's for $20,000, the most anyone in Hollywood had ever paid for an unproduced play.

facts.hook: The plane in Casablanca's final scene was cardboard, with little-person extras
facts.body: The background showing the airplane with people walking around it used little person extras and a proportionate cardboard plane. Fog was used to hide how unconvincing the model looked.

facts.hook: "As Time Goes By" stayed in Casablanca because Bergman had already cut her hair
facts.body: Max Steiner wanted to replace the song with his own, but Ingrid Bergman had cut her hair short for her next role, so the scenes could not be reshot. He based the whole score on it and "La Marseillaise".

facts.hook: Casablanca's last line was recorded a month after shooting ended
facts.body: Producer Wallis settled on "Louis, I think this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship" late, and Bogart was recalled to dub it a month after shooting had finished.

facts.hook: Chaplin's voice is heard for the first time in Modern Times, singing in gibberish
facts.body: He sings Léo Daniderff's "Je cherche après Titine" in a made-up language whose words seem to come from French and Italian.

facts.hook: The blindfolded skating scene in Modern Times was never dangerous
facts.body: The drop was matte-painted, and Chaplin skated on a plain floor with a ledge to tell him when to stop.

facts.hook: Modern Times was shot at 18 frames per second, which makes it look more frantic
facts.body: Most of the film was shot at "silent speed". Projected at "sound speed", 24 frames per second, the slapstick action looked even more frenetic.

facts.hook: Pan's Labyrinth's Pale Man has eyes in his hands, like a Japanese monster
facts.body: It is a feature shared by the Tenome, a Japanese mythological monster whose name means "hand eyes".

facts.hook: Voyager 1 got kitchen-grade aluminium foil on its cables just before launch
facts.body: Engineers had already hardened the design against Jupiter's radiation, but shortly before launch they still applied strips of kitchen-grade foil to certain cables for extra shielding.

facts.hook: Voyager 1's launch was saved with just 3.4 seconds of fuel to spare
facts.body: The Titan's second stage shut down early, so the Centaur stage had to burn much longer to make up for it. It finished just 3.4 seconds from running dry; on Voyager 2 the same failure would have left it short.

facts.hook: In 2017, Voyager 1 fired thrusters that hadn't been used since 1980
facts.body: Its usual jets had degraded, so the team switched to the trajectory correction thrusters, unused since 1980, to keep the antenna pointed at Earth.

facts.hook: After Saturn, Voyager 2's camera platform seized up
facts.body: The azimuth actuator of its scan platform seized, which cost some data and threatened the rest of the mission. Engineers sent a series of commands that got the platform working again.

facts.hook: The original tapes of the first moonwalk were probably erased
facts.body: Apollo 11 used slow-scan TV that was incompatible with broadcast TV. Copies in broadcast format survive, but the original recordings were likely wiped when NASA reused magnetic tape.

facts.hook: Armstrong took a piece of the 1903 Wright Flyer's propeller and wing to the Moon
facts.body: His personal-preference kit in the lunar module held a piece of wood from the Wright brothers' left propeller and a scrap of fabric from the wing of their plane.

facts.hook: Apollo 11's Columbia was named after a giant cannon in a Jules Verne novel
facts.body: The command module was named after the Columbiad, the giant cannon in From the Earth to the Moon. Collins later said the name was a reference to Christopher Columbus.

facts.hook: Apollo 13 beat its CO2 problem with manual covers and duct tape
facts.body: The lunar module's canisters couldn't support three astronauts, and the command module's didn't fit. Engineers on the ground designed an adapter from plastic covers ripped from manuals and duct tape.

facts.hook: On Apollo 13, each astronaut got just 200 ml of water a day
facts.body: With that tight ration the crew still came home with 12.8 kg of water left over, but the three astronauts lost 14 kg of body weight between them.

facts.hook: Apollo 13's plutonium cask sank 10 km to the bottom of the Tonga Trench
facts.body: The Atomic Energy Commission wanted the cask of plutonium oxide for the lunar generator to land somewhere safe, so the final course correction aimed for the Pacific. Later surveys found no radioactive leakage.

facts.hook: Sputnik 1's beeps would have revealed if a meteor had punctured it
facts.body: Its sphere was filled with pressurised nitrogen, and temperature and pressure were encoded in the length of its radio beeps. A pressure drop would have signalled a puncture.

facts.hook: In about three months, Sputnik 1 travelled some 70 million km around Earth
facts.body: It completed 1,440 orbits before burning up on re-entry on 4 January 1958. Its transmitter batteries were depleted after just three weeks.

facts.hook: Sputnik 2, Laika's ship, was designed and built in under four weeks
facts.body: Khrushchev wanted a "space spectacular" for the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution. According to Russian sources, the launch was approved on 10 or 12 October, and most of the spacecraft was built from rough sketches.

facts.hook: The USSR picked stray dogs for space, assuming they already knew cold and hunger
facts.body: Laika was a stray wandering the streets of Moscow. Soviet scientists assumed that street dogs had already learned to endure extreme cold and hunger.

facts.hook: Gagarin didn't land inside his capsule, and the USSR hid it at first
facts.body: He ejected at about 7,000 m, as planned, and came down by parachute. Because the FAI then required pilots to land with their craft, Soviet officials initially refused to admit it.

facts.hook: Vostok candidates could be no taller than 1.70 m; Gagarin was 1.57
facts.body: Chief engineer Korolev specified that candidates should weigh less than 72 kg and be no taller than 1.70 m, to fit in the cramped capsule.

facts.hook: Gagarin landed well once his instructor gave him a cushion to sit on
facts.body: At flight school he twice struggled to land and risked dismissal. His instructor gave him a cushion to improve his view from the cockpit, and he landed successfully.

facts.hook: The centre of mass of the Sun and Jupiter lies outside the Sun itself
facts.body: Jupiter is so massive that the point it shares with the Sun as a common centre of mass sits above the Sun's surface, by 7% of the Sun's radius.

facts.hook: Saturn has a hexagon at its north pole with sides longer than Earth is wide
facts.body: Voyager images first showed a hexagonal wave pattern around the north polar vortex. Unlike the other clouds, it does not shift in longitude.

facts.hook: Saturn is the only planet in the Solar System less dense than water
facts.body: Its average density is 0.69 g/cm³, about 30% less than water. Despite its huge size, its mass is only 95 times that of Earth.

facts.hook: Mars has almost as much surface area as all of Earth's dry land
facts.body: Mars is only about half Earth's diameter, yet its total surface area is just slightly less than the area of all of Earth's dry land.

facts.hook: From Mars, Phobos rises in the west, sets in the east and rises again 11 hours later
facts.body: Phobos moves differently from our Moon: seen from the surface of Mars, it rises in the west, sets in the east, and rises again in just 11 hours.

facts.hook: A Pluto-sized impact may have carved the basin covering 40% of Mars
facts.body: By this hypothesis, about four billion years ago a Pluto-sized body struck Mars and created the Borealis basin in the northern hemisphere.

facts.hook: On Mercury, one day from sunrise to sunrise lasts two Mercury years
facts.body: Its year lasts 88 Earth days, but one solar day lasts around 176: twice as long. Mercury spins three times for every two orbits of the Sun.

facts.hook: Seen from Mercury, the Sun stops in the sky and moves backwards
facts.body: Near perihelion, Mercury moves along its orbit faster than it spins. The Sun appears to halt in the sky and move backwards before its normal motion resumes.

facts.hook: A planet called Vulcan was proposed to explain Mercury's orbit
facts.body: Mercury's orbit showed a shift that Newtonian mechanics could not fully explain. A planet even closer to the Sun was proposed, but none was found; Einstein's relativity explained it.

facts.hook: Uranus was in a star catalogue 91 years before it was discovered as a planet
facts.body: In 1690, John Flamsteed observed it at least six times and logged it as 34 Tauri, as if it were a star. William Herschel spotted it in 1781 and at first reported it as a comet.

facts.hook: Herschel wanted to call the planet Uranus "George's Star"
facts.body: He named his find Georgium Sidus after his patron, King George III, who gave him an annual stipend of £200 on condition that he move to Windsor so the Royal Family could look through his telescopes.

facts.hook: Pluto appeared on photographic plates from 1909, but nobody recognised it until 1930
facts.body: Lowell's survey captured it in 1915 without anyone knowing what it was. Fourteen other precovery observations are known, the earliest from 1909. Tombaugh found it on 18 February 1930.

facts.hook: Two Uruguayan astronomers proposed the definition of planet that left Pluto out
facts.body: At the IAU meeting in 2006, Julio Ángel Fernández and Gonzalo Tancredi first proposed that a planet must have cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit. Pluto does not, so it became a dwarf planet.

facts.hook: Besides Earth, Titan is the only known world with stable liquid on its surface
facts.body: Titan, a moon of Saturn, has rivers, lakes and seas, but probably of liquid methane and ethane, not water.

facts.hook: A Spanish astronomer suspected in 1907 that Titan had an atmosphere
facts.body: Josep Comas i Solà saw Titan darken toward the edge of its disc, the first evidence of an atmosphere. Gerard Kuiper confirmed an atmosphere of methane in 1944 using spectroscopy.

facts.hook: Seen from Earth, the Sun is almost 13 billion times brighter than Sirius
facts.body: Sirius is the next brightest star in the sky, with an apparent magnitude of −1.46. The Sun, at −26.74, is by far the brightest object we see.

facts.hook: The Sun isn't yellow: seen from space, it is white
facts.body: With no atmosphere in the way, the Sun looks white. When it is very low in the sky, atmospheric scattering turns it yellow, red or orange.

facts.hook: The Sun spins faster at its equator: 25.6 days there, 33.5 at the poles
facts.body: It is not a solid body, so each region rotates at its own pace. This differential rotation is caused by convective motion and the Coriolis force.

facts.hook: In the 18th century, an English clergyman imagined a body that light could not leave
facts.body: John Michell, an astronomer and clergyman, proposed the idea in the late 18th century, and Pierre-Simon Laplace came up with it independently. Today we call such objects black holes.

facts.hook: Halley's Comet reflects only 4% of the sunlight it gets, like coal
facts.body: Astronomers expected it to reflect far more, but its nucleus turned out to be pitch black: it reflects about as little light as coal.

facts.hook: Halley predicted his comet's return but died 16 years before he could see it
facts.body: He worked out that the same comet returned about every 76 years. It was first seen again on 25 December 1758 by Johann Georg Palitzsch, a German farmer and amateur astronomer.

facts.hook: Halley's Comet circles the Sun in the opposite direction to the planets
facts.body: Its orbit is retrograde: it goes the opposite way to the planets and is inclined 18° to the ecliptic.

facts.hook: Before you were born, your liver was for a while your main red blood cell factory
facts.body: It happens during one stage of fetal development. Later in pregnancy, the bone marrow takes over.

facts.hook: The human foot has 26 bones and 33 joints
facts.body: It also has more than a hundred muscles, tendons and ligaments, making it a strong and complex mechanical structure.

facts.hook: The nail is much more permeable than skin
facts.body: It is often thought of as an impermeable barrier, but it is not. And 7 to 12% of the nail is water.

facts.hook: Fingernails grow up to four times faster than toenails
facts.body: Also, the nail of the index finger grows faster than that of the little finger.

facts.hook: Your bladder signals you when it holds 300 to 400 mL of urine
facts.body: The signal comes from stretch receptors in its wall, which activate once it reaches that volume.

facts.hook: A red blood cell lives about 120 days
facts.body: After that, organs such as the spleen and the liver break it down.

facts.hook: Blood makes up 7% of your body weight
facts.body: A little over half of that volume is plasma, the liquid part of blood.

facts.hook: Your mature red blood cells have no nucleus
facts.body: They also lack mitochondria and other organelles, which leaves as much room as possible for hemoglobin.

facts.hook: Your body has more than 600 skeletal muscles
facts.body: Together they make up around 40% of body weight in healthy young adults.

facts.hook: The femur averages 26.74% of a person's height
facts.body: In anthropology it is used to estimate someone's height from an incomplete skeleton.

facts.hook: In the umbilical cord, the vein carries oxygenated blood; the arteries, deoxygenated
facts.body: That is unusual in human anatomy; the pulmonary veins and arteries are another case. The names follow direction: the vein carries blood toward the fetus's heart.

facts.hook: Whether your earwax is wet or dry depends on a single change in one gene
facts.body: The wet type is dominant. A single base change in the ABCC11 gene makes the difference.

facts.hook: Platelets are fragments of other cells, called megakaryocytes
facts.body: They have no nucleus and, when a blood vessel is injured, they clump together to form a clot.

facts.hook: Your right lung has three lobes and your left lung only two
facts.body: Two fissures divide the right lung into three lobes; a single fissure divides the left one.

facts.hook: The smallest bone in the human body is the stapes, in the ear
facts.body: It measures about 3 mm at most.

facts.hook: 1 in 500 people has an extra rib in the neck
facts.body: It is called a cervical rib and can appear on one side or on both.

facts.hook: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body
facts.body: It is mostly mineral, mainly hydroxyapatite, with very little organic material.

facts.hook: Your body makes about 500 mL of cerebrospinal fluid a day but holds only 125–150 mL
facts.body: It surrounds the brain and spinal cord and acts as a shock absorber.

facts.hook: The Achilles tendon is the thickest tendon in the human body
facts.body: It connects the calf muscles to the calcaneus, the heel bone.

facts.hook: Your gut has its own nervous system, able to operate independently of the brain
facts.body: It is a mesh of neurons embedded in the lining of the digestive tract that governs, among other things, motility and secretion.

facts.hook: Goose bumps come from tiny muscles at the base of each hair contracting
facts.body: It can be triggered by cold or strong emotions. Some consider it a vestigial reflex in humans.

facts.hook: The 100,000 km capillary figure was based on an extraordinarily large person
facts.body: August Krogh worked it out in 1922 and it spread to many textbooks. More recent estimates give between 9,000 and 19,000 km.

facts.hook: The thymus's role in the immune system was discovered in 1961
facts.body: Until then it had been dismissed as an organ without functional importance.

facts.hook: Your heart beats on its own: nerves speed it up or slow it down, but don't control it
facts.body: Pacemaker cells in the heart itself set its rhythm. Sympathetic nerves raise the heart rate and the vagus nerve lowers it.

facts.hook: Your collarbone starts turning into bone before birth and finishes around age 21-25
facts.body: It is one of the first bones to start ossifying, around weeks 5-6 of gestation.

facts.hook: The hyoid bone in your neck touches no other bone; muscles and ligaments hold it
facts.body: It is horseshoe-shaped and helps with swallowing.

facts.hook: Before citrus arrived, ceviche’s ancestors were marinated in tumbo juice
facts.body: Before citrus reached the Andes in the 16th century, coastal people used juice from native plants such as the banana passionfruit, known locally as tumbo.

facts.hook: Early kimchi wasn't spicy: chili peppers only reached Korea in the early 1600s
facts.body: Chili peppers were a New World crop, unknown in Korea until the early 17th century. They did not become widespread in kimchi until the 19th century.

facts.hook: South Korea asked the US for help getting kimchi to its troops in Vietnam
facts.body: Its government wanted to guarantee supplies for soldiers who were reportedly "desperate" for the dish while serving in the field.

facts.hook: Soy sauce began as a way to stretch salt
facts.body: Salt was historically expensive. In ancient China under the Zhou dynasty, people already seasoned food with salted fermented fish that included soybeans.

facts.hook: Red gazpacho only appeared in the 19th century, when tomatoes were added
facts.body: Earlier gazpachos were made with stale bread, garlic, olive oil, salt and vinegar. Tomato joined the recipe only in the 19th century.

facts.hook: Gazpacho manchego is a hot meat stew, not a cold soup
facts.body: Despite the name, it is a hot stew whose main ingredients are small game such as rabbit or quail, and flatbread.

facts.hook: «Falafel» probably means «peppers» in Arabic
facts.body: It would be the plural of filfil, «pepper», a word borrowed from Persian. Another theory traces it to an Aramaic word for peppercorn.

facts.hook: Corn is cooked in lime or ash to loosen its hulls: that is nixtamalization
facts.body: The word comes from Nahuatl: nextli, "ash", and tamalli, a cooked corn dough.

facts.hook: The story that pizza Margherita was invented in 1889 for a queen is very doubtful
facts.body: Legend says pizzaiolo Raffaele Esposito made a red, white and green pizza for Queen Margherita. No media of the period reported the visit, and the story was first promoted in the 1930s–1940s.

facts.hook: «Sushi» means «sour»: its ancestors were fermented fish stored in rice
facts.body: The word literally means sour-tasting. Narezushi, fish stored in fermented rice for possibly months, is cited as one of its early influences.

facts.hook: Nigiri started out as fast food, in pieces much bigger than today’s
facts.body: It was the fast food of the chōnin class in the Edo period, and it became popular in Edo, today’s Tokyo, in the 1820s or 1830s.

facts.hook: The Maillard reaction helps brown crusts, coffee and dulce de leche
facts.body: The same chemistry darkens baked crusts, coffee roasts and dulce de leche, giving each its colour and flavour.

facts.hook: Farmed vanilla is pollinated by hand, and each flower lasts a day at most
facts.body: The flowers open in the morning and fade the same afternoon, so growers must pollinate them by hand.

facts.hook: Cocoa powder took off around 1828, with a press that squeezed out the cocoa butter
facts.body: It was Coenraad van Houten’s invention, and it laid the foundation for the modern solid chocolate industry. Until the 19th century, chocolate was a drink.

facts.hook: In Mesoamerica, chocolate was drunk, and flavored with chili
facts.body: It was flavored with additives such as vanilla, earflower and chili.

facts.hook: Tequila can only be made in Jalisco and parts of four other Mexican states
facts.body: By Mexican law it must be produced in Jalisco and in limited municipalities of Guanajuato, Michoacán, Nayarit and Tamaulipas.

facts.hook: Pink peppercorns aren't pepper: they come from a tree in another family
facts.body: They are the fruits of the Peruvian or the Brazilian pepper tree, plants of a different family (Anacardiaceae).

facts.hook: Birds don't feel the heat of chili peppers the way we do
facts.body: In mammals, capsaicin binds to pain receptors in the mouth. Birds lack a specific pain receptor, so they can eat some of the hottest peppers.

facts.hook: Some cheese rennet comes not from a calf’s stomach but from thistles
facts.body: Rennet was traditionally extracted from the stomachs of young calves, but some vegetarian rennets have been extracted from Cynara thistles.

facts.hook: Black tea gets its dark colour from letting the leaf oxidize fully
facts.body: Picked tea leaves soon oxidize and darken unless dried; black tea is the type that is fully oxidized.

facts.hook: Parícutin, a Mexican volcano, burst out of a farmer's cornfield in 1943
facts.body: The volcano surged suddenly from the cornfield of farmer Dionisio Pulido in 1943. It kept erupting until 1952, unusually long for this type of volcano.

facts.hook: Parícutin's lava buried two towns, but one church's ruins can still be visited
facts.body: Two towns were evacuated and buried by lava. Today visitors can still see the hardened, lava-covered ruins of the San Juan Parangaricutiro church.

facts.hook: Panama hats come from Ecuador; the name comes from where they were sold
facts.body: Straw hats woven in Ecuador were shipped first to the Isthmus of Panama before going on to buyers abroad. They took the name of the point of sale instead of their place of origin.

facts.hook: The tsunami from Chile's 1960 earthquake killed 61 people in Hawaii
facts.body: The earthquake, around magnitude 9.5, sent a tsunami across the Pacific that devastated Hilo, Hawaii, over 10,000 km from the epicenter and killed 61 people there.

facts.hook: Easter Island's moai had coral eyes with obsidian or red volcanic rock pupils
facts.body: Archaeologists found that the moai's eye sockets were designed to hold coral eyes, with either black obsidian or red scoria pupils.

facts.hook: Cajal and Golgi shared the 1906 Nobel while disagreeing about the nervous system
facts.body: Santiago Ramón y Cajal and Camillo Golgi shared the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Golgi supported reticular theory and disagreed with Cajal's neuron doctrine, which caused some controversy.

facts.hook: Syria and Lebanon drink mate, brought there by immigrants from Argentina
facts.body: Mate, the South American herbal drink, is also common in Lebanon and Syria, where it was brought by immigrants from Argentina.

facts.hook: The young love in Love in the Time of Cholera comes from the author's parents
facts.body: The young couple Fermina Daza and Florentino Ariza are based on García Márquez's parents. He said that once they married, they were no longer interesting as literary figures.

facts.hook: Chilean singer Violeta Parra showed her arpilleras at the Louvre's decorative arts museum
facts.body: Besides her music, Parra made arpilleras (embroidered tapestries), oil paintings and wire sculptures. In 1964 she became the first Latin American artist with a solo show at the Louvre's Museum of Decorative Arts.

facts.hook: Guarani is an official language of Paraguay, an Argentine province and Mercosur
facts.body: Guarani is one of Paraguay's two official languages, alongside Spanish. It is also official in Argentina's Corrientes province and one of Mercosur's three official languages, with Spanish and Portuguese.

facts.hook: In Oruro, an Andean festival banned in the 17th century survived as a Catholic rite
facts.body: The Spanish banned the native ceremonies in the 17th century, during their rule over Upper Peru. The Uru kept observing the festival in the form of a Catholic ritual on Candlemas.

facts.hook: Perito Moreno Glacier can raise a lake arm up to 30 m above the rest of the lake
facts.body: The glacier's advance blocks the Brazo Rico arm of Lake Argentino, whose water can rise up to 30 meters above the main lake. Eventually the pressure breaks through the ice in a spectacular rupture.

facts.hook: The word "mariachi" predates the French occupation said to have created it
facts.body: A popular story traced "mariachi" to the French intervention of the 1860s. Documents disproved it: a priest complained about the "mariachis" in an 1852 letter.

facts.hook: A historian says the Andean chullo hat mixes the Spanish birrete with the local hat
facts.body: According to Peruvian historian Arturo Jiménez Borja, the chullo comes from a cultural exchange: the Spaniards incorporated elements of their birretes into the original hat of the Andeans.

facts.hook: Tikal's king was killed on 14 January 378, the day "Fire Is Born" arrived
facts.body: The Maya king Chak Tok Ich'aak was killed on 14 January 378 AD. The same day, Siyaj K'ak' ("Fire Is Born"), probably a foreign general, arrived from the west.

facts.hook: Spain's first Christmas lottery draw was held in Cádiz in 1812
facts.body: The first Lotería Nacional draw held at Christmas took place on 18 December 1812 in Cádiz, and the grand prize went to number 03604.

facts.hook: In 1957, Buñol held a funeral for a tomato to protest the festival's ban
facts.body: With the festival banned, residents carried a coffin with a large tomato inside, followed by a band playing funeral marches. The protest worked and La Tomatina was finally permitted.

facts.hook: Elcano's coat of arms has a globe and the motto "You were the first to circumnavigate me"
facts.body: Charles V rewarded Elcano's feat with a coat of arms bearing a globe and the Latin motto Primus circumdedisti me, meaning "You were the first to circumnavigate me".

facts.hook: Argentine writer Julio Cortázar was born in Brussels during Belgium's German occupation
facts.body: Cortázar was born in Ixelles, Brussels, to Argentine parents. At the time, Belgium was occupied by German troops.

facts.hook: Capablanca said he learned chess at 4 watching his father, then beat him
facts.body: According to Capablanca, he learned chess at age four by watching his father play with friends. He pointed out an illegal move by his father and then beat him.

facts.hook: Two rivals objected to Cuba's Capablanca playing San Sebastián 1911; he won it
facts.body: At the 1911 San Sebastián tournament, Ossip Bernstein and Aron Nimzowitsch objected to Capablanca's participation because he had not fulfilled the entry condition. He went on to win the tournament.

facts.hook: Venezuela's Angel Falls are named after a U.S. aviator, not an angel
facts.body: The waterfall in Venezuela is named after Jimmie Angel, a U.S. aviator who flew over it in 1933. The name first appeared on a Venezuelan government map in 1939.

facts.hook: The pen name "Gabriela Mistral" reportedly honors poets D'Annunzio and Frédéric Mistral
facts.body: Chilean poet Lucila Godoy Alcayaga built her pseudonym from the names of two favorite poets, D'Annunzio and Frédéric Mistral, or, by another account, from the Archangel Gabriel and the mistral wind.

facts.hook: Buenos Aires' Teatro Colón stands where Argentina's first railway station once was
facts.body: The current Teatro Colón opened in 1908 on land that formerly housed the Park Station, the first railway station of the Argentine Republic.

facts.hook: The Spanish mop was inspired by how US hangars were cleaned
facts.body: While in the US, Spanish engineer Manuel Jalón saw hangars cleaned with a flat mop and a bucket with rollers. He took the idea back to Spain and began making roller buckets there.

facts.hook: The man credited with the mop also patented an improved disposable syringe
facts.body: His syringe had a plastic body, a plunger less prone to stick and thin walls that made disposal easier. It was made in Fraga, Spain, and exported to over 80 countries.

facts.hook: Peral's electric submarine made a simulated night attack without being noticed
facts.body: Isaac Peral's electric-powered submarine was launched in 1888. In a test with naval authorities, it made a simulated attack on a cruiser at night without being noticed.

facts.hook: Monturiol's first submarine grew out of watching coral harvesters at work
facts.body: In Cadaqués, Narcís Monturiol saw how dangerous coral harvesting was, and it set him thinking about travelling underwater. In 1859 his first submarine, Ictíneo I, made its first dive in Barcelona.

facts.hook: Several of Cierva's autogyros failed until he hinged the rotor blades
facts.body: His early autogyros struggled because the advancing and retreating blades produced uneven lift. A flapping hinge fixed this, and his first successful autogyro flew at Getafe, Spain, in 1923.

facts.hook: In 1906, a Spanish engineer steered a boat by wireless from shore before the king
facts.body: Leonardo Torres Quevedo's Telekino was an early wireless remote control. In Bilbao's port he guided a boat from the shore, with people on board, before King Alfonso XIII and a crowd.

facts.hook: The Spanish cable car over Niagara reached a century without notable accidents
facts.body: Leonardo Torres Quevedo's Spanish Aerocar was built between 1914 and 1916 over the Niagara Gorge in Canada. Its 100th anniversary, in 2016, marked a century of accident-free operation.

facts.hook: The first patented ballpoint pen, from 1888, never made it to market
facts.body: American inventor John J. Loud patented a pen with a small rotating steel ball. It had no commercial viability, and its patent eventually lapsed.

facts.hook: Argentina's "birome" pen is named after two partners, Bíró and Meyne
facts.body: László Bíró, his brother and their friend Juan Jorge Meyne sold their pen in Argentina as the "Birome", a blend of the surnames Bíró and Meyne. Argentines still call a ballpoint that.

facts.hook: In 1891, an Argentine police official started the first fingerprint files
facts.body: Juan Vucetich, an Argentine-Croatian police official, pioneered fingerprint identification. In 1891 he began the first filing of fingerprints, building on ideas of Francis Galton.

facts.hook: A rural doctor from La Pampa ended up standardizing coronary bypass surgery
facts.body: René Favaloro worked as the doctor of Jacinto Aráuz, a small town in La Pampa, Argentina, before leaving rural medicine. He went on to standardize coronary artery bypass surgery, the fundamental work of his career.

facts.hook: Post-its came from a failed attempt at a super-strong glue
facts.body: A 3M scientist aiming for a super-strong adhesive accidentally made a weak, reusable one. A colleague, Arthur Fry, later used it to anchor his bookmark in his hymn book.

facts.hook: Silly Putty came out of a search for a rubber substitute in wartime
facts.body: It was created during research into a potential rubber substitute for the United States in World War II. The result was a silicone toy with unusual physical properties.

facts.hook: Silly Putty could lift images off newspaper pages
facts.body: It could be used to transfer newspaper images to other surfaces. Newer papers with soy-based inks resist this more.

facts.hook: Salvador Dalí designed the Chupa Chups logo
facts.body: The logo of the lollipop brand, founded by Enric Bernat, was designed by the surrealist artist Salvador Dalí.

facts.hook: The Slinky began when a naval engineer saw a spring "step" off a shelf
facts.body: Richard James saw a spring "step" downward after being knocked off a shelf. He spent the next year testing steel wires until he found a spring that would "walk".

facts.hook: In the Vietnam War, the Slinky was used as a radio antenna
facts.body: Besides being a toy, the spring has served as a classroom teaching tool and as a portable, extendable radio antenna on the battlefield.

facts.hook: Play-Doh began as a soot cleaner for wallpaper
facts.body: It was first made in Cincinnati in the 1930s as a wallpaper cleaner, meant to remove coal residue. In the mid-1950s it was reworked and marketed to schools as a modeling compound.

facts.hook: The Frisbee business began with an offer of 25 cents for a 5-cent cake pan
facts.body: Walter Morrison and his future wife were tossing a cake pan on a beach near Los Angeles when someone offered 25 cents for it. A pan cost five cents, so he saw a business.

facts.hook: "Frisbee" comes from a pie company whose tins college students threw
facts.body: Wham-O's brand name for the disc came from the Frisbie Pie Company, a Connecticut pie maker whose empty tins college students were already tossing.

facts.hook: Long before Goodyear, Mesoamerican cultures cured rubber with plant juices
