facts.body: Ancient Mesoamerican cultures made balls, sandal soles, elastic bands and waterproof containers from rubber. They cured it with plant juices, an early form of vulcanization.

facts.hook: Teflon was found because a gas bottle stopped flowing before it was empty
facts.body: In 1938, DuPont's Roy Plunkett saw gas stop flowing from a bottle that should not yet have been empty. Chemists sawed it open and found a waxy, oddly slippery white coating: PTFE, now known as Teflon.

facts.hook: The oldest known mention of fried potatoes comes from a Chilean book of 1673
facts.body: In "Happy Captivity", Chilean soldier Francisco Núñez de Pineda recounts being held by the Mapuche in 1629. He mentions papas fritas, fried potatoes, among the food.

facts.hook: Rubik didn't see his cube was a puzzle until he scrambled it
facts.body: Ernő Rubik wanted to solve an engineering problem: letting small parts move independently without the whole mechanism falling apart. Only after scrambling his new cube did he realise he had made a puzzle.

facts.hook: A Japanese engineer patented a near-identical mechanism to Rubik's Cube in 1976
facts.body: Terutoshi Ishigi, a self-taught engineer and ironworks owner near Tokyo, was granted a Japanese patent in 1976. His patent is generally accepted as an independent reinvention.

facts.hook: China was already making toilet paper on a huge scale in the 14th century
facts.body: In the early 14th century, the area of today's Zhejiang alone produced ten million packages of 1,000 to 10,000 sheets of toilet paper a year.

facts.hook: In 1393, the family of China's Hongwu Emperor used perfumed toilet paper
facts.body: Records of the Imperial Bureau of Supplies note 15,000 sheets of special soft-fabric toilet paper made for the imperial family alone, each one perfumed.

facts.hook: An Argentine mechanic devised a childbirth aid after seeing how to pull out a cork
facts.body: Jorge Odón saw a YouTube party trick that uses an inflated plastic bag to remove a cork trapped in a bottle. He imagined using it in difficult births and tested a prototype with a doll in a glass jar.

facts.hook: Josephine Cochrane devised her dishwasher so servants would not damage her china
facts.body: In 1886, wealthy Josephine Cochrane and mechanic George Butters built a hand-powered dishwasher to protect her good china. It was unveiled at the 1893 World's Fair in Chicago.

facts.hook: Mary Anderson is popularly credited with the first working wiper, but there were others
facts.body: Her design was worked by a lever from inside the vehicle. But at least three inventors, her included, patented windscreen cleaning devices around the same time, in 1903.

facts.hook: Robert Kearns sued Ford over his intermittent wiper, and won
facts.body: Kearns showed his wiper design to Ford and proposed that it manufacture it. He later sued Ford and eventually won, and the dispute inspired the 2008 film Flash of Genius.

facts.hook: Tetra Pak's first cartons were tetrahedrons, and that is where the name comes from
facts.body: The company's name derives from its original tetrahedron-shaped, plastic-coated paper carton. The rectangular Tetra Brik was launched in 1963.

facts.hook: Lemmings don't leap into the sea in a mass suicide
facts.body: The myth spread especially after Disney's 1958 film White Wilderness. Some lemmings migrate in large groups, but it is not a deliberate mass suicide in which animals choose to die.

facts.hook: Ostriches don't bury their heads in the sand when in danger
facts.body: That is a popular assumption, but it is false. When threatened, an ostrich will lie flat against the ground or run away, and if cornered it can attack with a kick of its powerful legs.

facts.hook: Bumblebees were said to be unable to fly, but they fly just fine
facts.body: According to 20th-century folklore, aerodynamics proved the bumblebee should be incapable of flight. More sophisticated analysis shows it can fly because its wings encounter dynamic stall on every oscillation.

facts.hook: It's a myth that Columbus defied a belief in a flat Earth
facts.body: Washington Irving's 1828 biography popularized the idea that Columbus struggled against people who insisted the Earth was flat. It is a popular misconception: scholars had known it was spherical since antiquity.

facts.hook: George Washington's false teeth were not made of wood
facts.body: Washington had several sets of false teeth and, contrary to common lore, none were made of wood. They were made of materials such as metal, ivory, bone and animal teeth.

facts.hook: Nobody says 'Play it again, Sam' in Casablanca
facts.body: The line most closely tied to the film is not spoken in it. Ilsa asks Sam, 'Play it once, Sam, for old times' sake,' and then, 'Play it, Sam.'

facts.hook: Not every ant colony has just one queen: some have several, others none
facts.body: Contrary to popular belief, some ant nests have multiple queens and others can exist without any. In queenless colonies, some workers can reproduce.

facts.hook: Listening to Mozart doesn't make you smarter, despite the headlines
facts.body: A 1993 study reported a short-term boost on certain mental tasks, which the press exaggerated into 'Mozart makes you smart'. The author of the study stresses it has no effect on general intelligence.

facts.hook: Coca-Cola didn't invent Santa Claus or his red-and-white suit
facts.body: Haddon Sundblom's 1930s Coca-Cola ads spawned urban legends that the company invented Santa or chose his colours for its brand. But Santa had appeared in red and white long before, on magazine covers.

facts.hook: Cinco de Mayo is not Mexico's Independence Day
facts.body: It is often believed in the US to be Mexico's national day, but it is not. It marks the anniversary of the Battle of Puebla, fought on 5 May 1862.

facts.hook: A Roman 'vomitorium' wasn't for vomiting: it was an exit passage
facts.body: It is a common misconception that Romans had rooms for vomiting so they could keep eating. A vomitorium is a passage below or behind the seats through which large crowds can exit rapidly.

facts.hook: Michelangelo didn't paint the Sistine ceiling lying on his back
facts.body: The popular image of him lying on the scaffold is wrong. He painted standing up, from a flat wooden platform built on brackets near the top of the windows.

facts.hook: Dr. Guillotin was not executed by the guillotine
facts.body: The claim that he died on the machine named after him is wrong: he died at home of a carbuncle. A different Guillotin, a doctor from Lyon, was executed by it, which may have fed the confusion.

facts.hook: The Inuit don't have a huge number of words for snow, just a few roots
facts.body: The popular belief comes from a misunderstanding of polysynthetic languages. Inuit builds long words by adding descriptive affixes to a few base roots, much as English uses adjectives.

facts.hook: No evidence that pepper was used in the Middle Ages to hide rotten meat
facts.body: It is commonly believed, but historians view it as highly unlikely. In the Middle Ages pepper was a luxury item, affordable only to the wealthy, who had unspoiled meat available.

facts.hook: The 'lead' in a pencil isn't lead at all; it's graphite
facts.body: Chemists once thought graphite was a form of lead and named it plumbago. The core is still called 'lead' in English, though it never contained the element.

facts.hook: There is no evidence that Vikings wore horned helmets
facts.body: The horned helmet is a 19th-century image. Horned helmets would have been cumbersome and hazardous in the close-quarters style of Viking combat.

facts.hook: There's no evidence Marie Antoinette ever said 'Let them eat cake'
facts.body: It is often attributed to her, but there is no evidence she said it. Rousseau had already put it in the mouth of 'a great princess', in a text written before she arrived in France.

facts.hook: A camel's hump stores fat, not water
facts.body: It is a common myth that camels store water in their humps. The hump is a reservoir of fatty tissue that serves as a calorie reserve, not as a water supply.

facts.hook: Pando, a Utah aspen grove of about 47,000 trunks, is a single organism
facts.body: Its stems are genetically identical and linked by one root system spanning 42.8 ha. It is generally held to be the largest organism by weight.

facts.hook: The Árbol del Tule in Mexico has the stoutest trunk of any tree
facts.body: It stands in the church grounds of Santa María del Tule, in the Mexican state of Oaxaca.

facts.hook: The bee orchid's flower mimics a female bee and lures the males
facts.body: Its lip acts as a decoy that male bees mistake for a female. In the Mediterranean it is pollinated by Eucera bees.

facts.hook: The Rafflesia flower stinks of rotting flesh and lasts only a few days
facts.body: The buds take many months to develop. Then the flower lasts for just a few days.

facts.hook: In 1811, a botanist picked up a curiously shaped pebble that turned out to be a plant
facts.body: It was a Lithops, or living stone. William John Burchell made the first scientific description of these plants, which are camouflaged as small stones.

facts.hook: The Mariana Trench's deepest point is over 2 km farther down than Everest's peak is up
facts.body: The deepest point of the trench, known as the Challenger Deep, lies more than 2 km farther from sea level than the peak of Mount Everest does.

facts.hook: A flatfish seen in the Mariana Trench in 1960 may really have been a sea cucumber
facts.body: The 1960 expedition claimed to see a flatfish about 30 cm long. Many marine biologists are now skeptical and suggest the creature may instead have been a sea cucumber.

facts.hook: The giant squid floats with ammonium chloride instead of a gas-filled bladder
facts.body: Giant squid keep neutral buoyancy with an ammonium chloride solution found throughout their bodies, unlike most fish, which use a gas-filled swim bladder.

facts.hook: In 1513, the Gulf Stream pushed Ponce de León's ship backwards despite the wind
facts.body: The voyage log noted that the ship could not move forwards, only backwards, because the current was more powerful than the wind. This is how Europeans discovered the Gulf Stream.

facts.hook: Whalers located the Gulf Stream by watching the whales
facts.body: Whale behaviour, along with water temperature and colour, gave the current away. American merchant ships crossed it, while British mail ships sailed against it and took weeks longer.

facts.hook: At 2,500 m, a bacterium photosynthesizes using the faint glow of a black smoker
facts.body: Near a black smoker off the coast of Mexico lives a bacterium of the Chlorobiaceae family that uses its faint glow, because no sunlight reaches that depth.

facts.hook: A hydrothermal vent snail hardens its body with iron sulfides, not calcium
facts.body: It is the scaly-foot, a gastropod that uses pyrite and greigite, two iron sulfides, for its hardened body parts instead of calcium carbonate.

facts.hook: The living part of the Great Barrier Reef may be only 6,000 to 8,000 years old
facts.body: That is the estimate of a reef research centre for the living structure of the world's largest coral reef system.

facts.hook: In 2020 a previously unknown 500 m tall reef was found in the Great Barrier Reef
facts.body: Nobody knew it was there. It lies in the northern area of the system and is 1.5 km wide at its base.

facts.hook: A great white swam 20,000 km to Australia and back in under nine months
facts.body: A shark from South Africa was tracked swimming to Australia's northwestern coast and back.

facts.hook: Great white sharks have no third eyelid: they roll their eyes back to protect them
facts.body: Instead, well-developed eye muscles let them roll each eye back into its socket to keep it safe from attacks.

facts.hook: In the Sargasso Sea, ships were trapped by calm winds, not by the seaweed
facts.body: Sargassum masses are generally not a threat to ships. Historic cases of sailing ships trapped there are due to often-calm winds.

facts.hook: Nearly half the mass of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is fishing nets
facts.body: A study found that synthetic fishing nets made up nearly half of the mass of this area of plastic in the North Pacific.

facts.hook: The Trieste, the bathyscaphe that dove to the Challenger Deep, floated on gasoline
facts.body: Its buoyancy tanks were filled with gasoline, which floats in water and is similarly incompressible.

facts.hook: The colossal squid is believed to have the largest eyes in the animal kingdom
facts.body: Each of its eyes also carries light-producing organs called photophores.

facts.hook: Colossal squid tentacles carry swiveling hooks as well as suckers
facts.body: Its arms and tentacles are armed with hooks, some of which can swivel while others have three points.

facts.hook: A Greenland shark may take around 150 years to reach sexual maturity
facts.body: It grows very slowly, about 0.5 to 1 cm a year, and can live for centuries.

facts.hook: A parasite on Greenland sharks' eyes may act as a lure for their prey
facts.body: It is a copepod that attaches itself to the shark's eyes. It may glow and so attract prey, but this has not been verified.

facts.hook: The vampire squid has no ink and releases a cloud of glowing mucus
facts.body: If highly agitated, it ejects sticky bioluminescent mucus with countless orbs of light from its arm tips. The glowing cloud may last nearly 10 minutes.

facts.hook: The vampire squid breathes in water with only 3% oxygen saturation
facts.body: It lives in the oxygen minimum zone, where oxygen is too low for most complex organisms that depend on it. No other cephalopod can live its whole life there.

facts.hook: A 325 BC account describes frozen water “on which one can neither walk nor sail”
facts.body: It is Pytheas of Massilia's account of a journey north, to a land where the Sun set only three hours a day. He was probably describing floating ice.

facts.hook: 55 million years ago, the Arctic grew warm enough to host tropical life
facts.body: During the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, surface waters of the far north warmed, seasonally at least, enough for dinoflagellates that need over 22 °C.

facts.hook: Sailors' tales of rogue waves were taken for myth until they were measured
facts.body: Mariners' accounts and ship damage had long suggested they exist. In 1995, a wave measured at the Draupner platform in the North Sea caused minor damage that confirmed the reading.

facts.hook: The ocean sunfish, known for basking, spends much of its life below 200 m
facts.body: Although it is thought to spend much of its time basking at the surface, research indicates adults spend a large portion of their lives at depths greater than 200 m.

facts.hook: The ocean sunfish can produce up to 300 million eggs, more than any known vertebrate
facts.body: It is the females that do it, and no other known vertebrate produces as many.

facts.hook: The largest living turtle has no bony shell
facts.body: It is the leatherback. Instead of hard scutes, it has thick, leathery skin, one of the traits that set it apart from other sea turtles.

facts.hook: Lloyd's of London does not charge extra to sail through the Bermuda Triangle
facts.body: Lloyd's found that unusually large numbers of ships had not sunk there, and United States Coast Guard records confirm it.

facts.hook: The Red Sea is still widening and, by one model, will become an ocean
facts.body: It formed when the Arabian Peninsula split from the Horn of Africa, and the widening continues.

facts.hook: Tierra del Fuego got its name from fires Magellan saw from the sea
facts.body: The fires were lit by the Indigenous inhabitants. Magellan, sailing for the Spanish Crown, gave the land its name in 1520.

facts.hook: In some Baarle restaurants, switching tables meant switching countries
facts.body: At one time, Dutch restaurants had to close earlier than Belgian ones. For restaurants right on the border, customers simply moved to a table on the Belgian side.

facts.hook: In 1918, 96% of Büsingen's voters chose Switzerland, yet the village stayed German
facts.body: Switzerland could not offer anything suitable in exchange, so no land changed hands. Büsingen is still a German exclave, entirely surrounded by Swiss territory.

facts.hook: Büsingen, a German village, has two postal codes: one German, one Swiss
facts.body: Letters can use either country's code, and residents can have a German or a Swiss phone number. The village even has its own licence plate, BÜS.

facts.hook: Before humans arrived, the Canaries had giant lizards, rats and tortoises
facts.body: They were endemic animals, now extinct, such as the giant lizard Gallotia goliath or the Tenerife and Gran Canaria giant rats.

facts.hook: The Argentina–Brazil border runs through a waterfall, the Devil's Throat
facts.body: It is the part of Iguazu Falls that carries the most water: about half of the river's flow.

facts.hook: Bolivia's Cerro Rico is considered the richest source of silver in history
facts.body: It is an Andean mountain near the Bolivian city of Potosí. Mining there began in 1545, under the Spanish Empire.

facts.hook: The Vatican has its own railway station
facts.body: A short spur links it to Italy's rail network at Rome's Roma San Pietro station.

facts.hook: Dallol, in Ethiopia, has green acid ponds with a pH below 1
facts.body: Its name comes from the Afar people and means dissolution or disintegration. The landscape mixes acid ponds, iron oxide, sulfur and salt plains.

facts.hook: A river island is run by France for half the year and by Spain for the other half
facts.body: It is Pheasant Island, under joint Spanish and French sovereignty, the world's smallest condominium. France runs it from August to January and Spain from February to July.

facts.hook: Easter Island got its name because a navigator arrived on Easter Sunday 1722
facts.body: Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen reached it on Easter Sunday, 5 April 1722, and named it Paasch-Eyland, 18th-century Dutch for "Easter Island".

facts.hook: In 1946 the Faroes narrowly voted for independence, and Denmark annulled the declaration
facts.body: The vote was 50.73% to 49.27%. Independence was declared on 18 September, and Denmark annulled the declaration on 20 September.

facts.hook: Kiribati has islands in all four hemispheres
facts.body: Its land totals just 811 km², spread over more than three million square kilometres of ocean.

facts.hook: In 1995 Kiribati moved the date line so the whole country shares the same day
facts.body: Until then the date line divided the country. It was shifted east so its easternmost islands, the Line Islands, would share the same day as the rest.

facts.hook: Lake Baikal is estimated to be 25 to 30 million years old
facts.body: That makes it one of the oldest lakes in geological terms. Unlike other large high-latitude lakes, its sediments were never scoured by continental ice sheets.

facts.hook: On Lake Titicaca, the Uros live on floating islands they build from totora
facts.body: Totora is a thick, buoyant sedge. The Uros also use it for the buildings on the islands.

facts.hook: In Bolivia's Llanos de Moxos, ancient peoples farmed on raised fields they built
facts.body: They also built canals, causeways and mounds. These earthworks may be spread over some 50,000 km².

facts.hook: Llívia is a Spanish enclave inside France because it was a town, not a village
facts.body: The Treaty of the Pyrenees (1659) ceded only villages to France. Llívia counted as a town, so it stayed Spanish.

facts.hook: Egyptians used asphalt from the Dead Sea for mummification
facts.body: From deep seeps, the lake constantly spits up lumps of black asphalt. Egyptian embalmers imported it from the Dead Sea region.

facts.hook: The Dead Sea is what is left of a lake whose level once stood 250 m higher
facts.body: It was Lake Lisan. From 70,000 to 12,000 years ago its level was 100 to 250 m higher, peaking around 26,000 years ago. Then it shrank and became saltier.

facts.hook: A Swiss traveller dressed as a local rediscovered Petra for the West in 1812
facts.body: He went by Sheikh Ibrahim. Until then, the old Nabataean capital had been unknown to the Western world.

facts.hook: Venezuela's Catatumbo lightning once guided ships like a lighthouse
facts.body: For centuries it was known as the "Lighthouse of Maracaibo", after the Venezuelan lake where it occurs.

facts.hook: Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni is so flat that it is ideal for calibrating satellites
facts.body: Across hundreds of square kilometres of salt, its height varies by less than a metre. The flat covers more than 10,000 km².

facts.hook: The last German troops to surrender in the Second World War were on Svalbard
facts.body: They were soldiers at a German weather station. They surrendered on 4 September 1945, months after Germany's own surrender.

facts.hook: The world heat record, 56.7 °C in Death Valley in 1913, is in doubt
facts.body: The World Meteorological Organization accepts it, but some modern experts dispute the 1913 reading because of observer issues.

facts.hook: The largest human-made explosion could have been twice as big: it was scaled back
facts.body: In 1961 the Soviet Union tested the Tsar Bomba at 50 megatons. Its design allowed over 100, but the uranium tamper was swapped for lead to reduce radioactive fallout.

facts.hook: The Tsar Bomba's blast wave circled the Earth three times
facts.body: The 1961 Soviet test over the Novaya Zemlya archipelago was so powerful that its blast wave circled the globe three times.

facts.hook: The Eiffel Tower was the world's tallest structure for 41 years
facts.body: Completed in 1889, it held the title of tallest human-made structure for 41 years, until the Chrysler Building rose in New York.

facts.hook: The Empire State added a 61 m "crown" over fear of a Chrysler trick
facts.body: On the first plans it would top the Chrysler Building by only 1.2 m. Fearing a last-minute trick, Raskob had the design revised once more, adding a 61 m crown and a mooring mast for airships.

facts.hook: The Empire State was the first building in the world with over 100 floors
facts.body: It opened on 1 May 1931 and broke the 100-story barrier.

facts.hook: The Saturn V dwarfed every rocket successfully flown before it
facts.body: It stood 111 m tall and, fully fueled, had a mass of nearly 3,000 tonnes: no rocket successfully flown until then came close in size.

facts.hook: The Cullinan diamond, found in 1905, weighed 621.2 grams in the rough
facts.body: That is 3,106 carats. When it turned up at the Premier mine in South Africa, it was the largest gem-quality rough diamond found up to then. It is named after the mine owner, Thomas Cullinan.

facts.hook: The Cullinan diamond travelled in a coat pocket while a warship carried a decoy
facts.body: In 1908 Abraham Asscher collected the diamond in London and returned to the Netherlands by train and ferry with it in his coat. Meanwhile a Royal Navy ship crossed the North Sea with an empty box.

facts.hook: Concorde linked Paris and New York in about 3.5 hours; other jets took 8
facts.body: From 1976 to 2003 the supersonic Concorde crossed the Atlantic in just under three and a half hours on average. Subsonic airliners took about eight.

facts.hook: The strongest earthquake ever recorded hit less than 20 minutes after another one
facts.body: Chile, 22 May 1960: at 14:55 another quake hit the south of the country, and about 15 minutes later the Valdivia quake began, at around magnitude 9.5 (9.4-9.6 in most studies). As of 2026 it is the strongest ever recorded.

facts.hook: The Hindenburg floated on flammable hydrogen but had a smoking room
facts.body: Along with its twin, it was the largest airship ever built by volume. It was meant to use helium, but a US export ban forced a switch to flammable hydrogen. Even so, the airship had a smoking room.

facts.hook: In the Carboniferous, a dragonfly relative flew on wings about 70 cm across
facts.body: Meganeura is one of the largest known insects. It hunted other insects, and its fossils were first found in France in 1880.

facts.hook: Argentinosaurus, one of the largest known land animals, is known only from fragments
facts.body: So its exact size is hard to pin down: length estimates range from 30 to 39.7 metres. It lived in what is now Argentina.

facts.hook: Quetzalcoatlus was first put at over 15 m across; now, about 10-11 m
facts.body: Early calculations gave it a wingspan of over 15 m. Recent estimates put it at around 10-11 m, though it is still among the largest flying animals known.

facts.hook: The snake Titanoboa reached about 12.8 m, but may have eaten mostly fish
facts.body: It lived in South America around 60 million years ago and is estimated at up to 12.8 m long. Despite its size, there are signs that it ate mainly fish.

facts.hook: The largest seaplane ever built flew only once, at 21 m up
facts.body: The Hughes H-4 Hercules lifted off the water on 2 November 1947, with Howard Hughes at the controls. Only the prototype was ever built, and it never flew again.

facts.hook: The biggest aircraft of its day was built mostly of wood, because of the war
facts.body: The H-4 Hercules was meant to carry 750 fully equipped troops. Because of wartime restrictions on aluminium, it was built mostly of wood.

facts.hook: In 1974 an SR-71 flew between New York and London in 1 h 54 min 56 s
facts.body: The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird, a Mach 3+ reconnaissance aircraft, set that record in 1974: under two hours between the two cities.

facts.hook: The SR-71 leaked fuel on the ground: its panels only fit when hot in flight
facts.body: Its fuselage panels sat loose on the ground and only aligned as the airframe heated up. Because of this, and the lack of a seal able to cope with the heat, JP-7 fuel leaked onto the runway before takeoff.

facts.hook: The world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall is named after a pilot
facts.body: Venezuela's Angel Falls has a plunge of 807 m (979 m in total). It is named after US aviator Jimmie Angel, who flew over it in 1933.

facts.hook: The deepest hole ever drilled by humans was halted in 1992: it was hotter than expected
facts.body: The SG-3 borehole in Russia's Kola Peninsula was meant to reach 15,000 m but stalled at 12,262 m: the rock was far hotter than expected. As of 2026 it is still the deepest human-made hole.

facts.hook: A 458 m tanker was too big for the Suez, Panama and English Channel routes
facts.body: The supertanker Seawise Giant, later Knock Nevis, was 458 m long and the largest ship of her time. She was so big that she could not use those three waterways.

facts.hook: In 1979 Typhoon Tip set the record-low sea-level pressure: 870 hPa
facts.body: A reconnaissance aircraft measured it on 12 October, about 840 km from Guam. At its peak, Tip was also the largest tropical cyclone on record.

facts.hook: A single aircraft, the Antonov An-225, set 240 world records
facts.body: It was the heaviest aircraft ever built, with a maximum takeoff weight of 640 tonnes, and set 240 world records.

facts.hook: Rome's Pantheon still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome, after almost 2,000 years
facts.body: Its concrete dome has an interior height to the oculus equal to its diameter: 43 metres.

facts.hook: The world's largest pyramid isn't Egyptian: it's in Cholula, Mexico
facts.body: It is the largest pyramid by volume known today, though not the tallest. In Nahuatl it is Tlachihualtepetl, "constructed mountain", and today it looks like a hill with a church on top.

facts.hook: Krakatoa erupted in 1883 and people 4,800 km away took it for cannon fire
facts.body: Its third explosion is considered the loudest known sound in history. It was heard in Perth, Australia, 3,110 km away, and on Rodrigues, near Mauritius, 4,800 km away, where it was taken for cannon fire from a nearby ship.

facts.hook: The Great Eastern was the largest ship ever built when launched in 1858
facts.body: She was designed to carry 4,000 passengers on very long voyages without refuelling.

facts.hook: A stretch of the world's longest artificial waterway was begun in 486 BC
facts.body: It is China's Grand Canal, which grew over centuries. The Han Canal, its second-oldest section, was begun south of Yangzhou and within three years linked the Yangtze and Huai rivers.

facts.hook: For centuries, the Lighthouse of Alexandria was one of the tallest human-made structures
facts.body: Ptolemaic Egypt built it in the 3rd century BC, during the reign of Ptolemy II, and it is estimated to have been at least 100 metres tall.

facts.hook: The Colossus of Rhodes, about 33 m tall, was the tallest statue of the ancient world
facts.body: It stood near the Rhodes harbour entrance on a 15 m white marble pedestal. An earthquake brought it down in 226 BC.

facts.hook: Titanic beat its twin Olympic as the largest ship by being slightly heavier
facts.body: Titanic was slightly heavier than its twin Olympic, which let it claim the title of largest ship afloat once it was finished.

facts.hook: Two metal plates 10 nm apart are pushed together with about one atmosphere of pressure
facts.body: This is the Casimir effect, from quantum field theory. Its strength falls off rapidly with distance, but at submicron scales it becomes the dominant force between uncharged conductors.

facts.hook: In 1798, Henry Cavendish worked out the mass of the Earth with a torsion balance
facts.body: His result was expressed as the density of the Earth, or equivalently its mass. It also gave the first accurate value of the gravitational constant G, though G does not appear explicitly in his work: one of the first references to it came in 1873.

facts.hook: A water drop that vaporized almost at once at 168 °C lasted 152 seconds at 202 °C
facts.body: Victorian boiler designer William Fairbairn cited it. This is the Leidenfrost effect: the bottom of the drop vaporizes on contact and the steam, a much poorer heat conductor, insulates it.

facts.hook: In many real-life datasets, the first digit is 1 far more often than the others
facts.body: Small leading digits are the most likely. Simon Newcomb noticed it in 1881: the early pages of logarithm tables, starting with 1, were much more worn. It shows up in electricity bills, stock prices or lengths of rivers.

facts.hook: In math, a ball can be cut into five pieces and reassembled into two copies of itself
facts.body: You only move and rotate them. It seems impossible, since that ought to preserve volume, but the pieces are non-measurable sets: collections of points with no volume in the ordinary sense. Fewer than five will not do.

facts.hook: Graham's number is so huge that its digits would not fit in the observable universe
facts.body: It arose as an upper bound on a problem in Ramsey theory, a field of mathematics. Even if each digit took up one tiny Planck volume, the observable universe would be far too small to write it out.

facts.hook: That four colors suffice for any map was only proved in 1976, with a computer
facts.body: It was first posed in 1852: coloring a map so that no two neighboring regions share a color. Appel and Haken proved it with a computer, and it was controversial because no human could check it by hand. In 2005 it was verified with theorem-proving software.

facts.hook: St. Elmo's fire is not fire but plasma, glowing on masts and spires during thunderstorms
facts.body: The electric field around pointed objects like masts ionizes the air and produces a blue or violet glow. Sailors regarded it with awe, and it can warn of an imminent lightning strike.

facts.hook: In certain systems, a negative temperature in kelvin is hotter than any positive one
facts.body: It is not colder than absolute zero: if a negative-temperature system touches a positive-temperature one, heat flows from the negative to the positive. It only happens in systems with an energy ceiling.

facts.hook: The butterfly effect was once a seagull: Lorenz was persuaded to make it more poetic
facts.body: Lorenz originally used a seagull causing a storm, but was persuaded to switch to a butterfly and a tornado by 1972. The idea: a tornado's exact path can be influenced by a distant butterfly flapping its wings weeks earlier.

facts.hook: The butterfly effect was found by rounding: Lorenz typed 0.506 instead of 0.506127
facts.body: To redo a weather run, Lorenz entered the value from the printout instead of the full-precision one. The result was a completely different weather scenario.

facts.hook: The Möbius strip was "discovered" in 1858, but it already appeared in Roman mosaics
facts.body: Möbius and Listing discovered it independently in 1858. It had been known long before: it can be seen in several Roman mosaics from the third century CE, although in some the twist may be a coincidence.

facts.hook: Cut a Möbius strip lengthwise down the middle and you get one longer strip, not two
facts.body: You get one long strip with four half-twists, still in one piece. Cut that one again along its centerline and you do get two strips, linked together.

facts.hook: Aerogel was born from a 1931 bet: swap the liquid in a gel for gas
facts.body: Kistler bet Charles Learned over who could replace the liquid in jellies with gas without causing shrinkage. The result is a solid of extremely low density and extremely low thermal conductivity.

facts.hook: An aerogel, though solid, can be up to 99.98% air
facts.body: It is a solid, rigid and dry material, made from a gel whose liquid has been replaced by a gas. Its air pockets take up most of the space inside it.

facts.hook: A current in a loop of superconducting wire can persist indefinitely with no power source
facts.body: In a superconductor the resistance drops abruptly to zero below its critical temperature, unlike an ordinary metallic conductor, whose resistance only decreases gradually.

facts.hook: Ferrofluid, a liquid drawn to magnets, was invented in 1963 as zero-gravity rocket fuel
facts.body: It is made of tiny magnetic particles suspended in a fluid such as water. NASA's Steve Papell devised it to make rocket fuel that a magnetic field could draw toward the fuel pump in weightlessness.

facts.hook: The chess queen gained her modern power in the late 1400s, probably in Valencia
facts.body: In the late 15th century the pawn, bishop and queen gained their modern moves, and the queen became the most powerful piece. The new rules probably appeared first in Valencia, Spain, around 1475.

facts.hook: The first basketball hoops were peach baskets
facts.body: In 1891 James Naismith wanted an indoor game for the long New England winters. For a goal he nailed a peach basket onto an elevated track at the gym.

facts.hook: The basketball backboard was invented to stop spectators interfering with shots
facts.body: The first baskets were nailed to a balcony, and fans up there could interfere with shots. The backboard prevented that and, as a bonus, made rebound shots possible.

facts.hook: Only four European teams went to the first World Cup, Uruguay 1930
facts.body: Many European teams stayed away because of the long trip to South America during the Great Depression. In the end only Belgium, France, Romania and Yugoslavia went, crossing by sea.

facts.hook: The 1930 World Cup had no qualifiers: accepting the invitation was enough
facts.body: Every FIFA member was invited and had until 28 February 1930 to accept. In the end 13 teams took part.

facts.hook: The 1950 World Cup had no final: the champion came out of a league round
facts.body: After the first round, the four group winners played a round-robin. Uruguay beat Brazil in the deciding match, the Maracanazo, and took the title.

facts.hook: A dog named Pickles found the World Cup trophy stolen in 1966
facts.body: Before the 1966 World Cup, the Jules Rimet trophy was stolen from an exhibition. A dog named Pickles found it in a London garden and became the tournament's unusual hero.

facts.hook: A Test cricket match can last five days and still end with no winner
facts.body: Test matches are played over five days. If time runs out before either side can win, the match is declared a draw, with no winner.

facts.hook: Golf went 112 years without being Olympic: out after 1904, back in Rio 2016
facts.body: Golf was on the Olympic programme in 1900 and 1904, then returned to the Games at Rio 2016 after a 112-year absence.

facts.hook: The oldest known rubber balls were found in a sacrificial bog linked to the Olmecs
facts.body: At El Manatí, an early Olmec-associated site, a dozen balls 10 to 22 cm across have been recovered. Five date to about 1700–1600 BC.

facts.hook: The ball in the Mesoamerican ballgame could weigh as much as about 4 kg
facts.body: It was made of solid rubber and, in the most common theory, players struck it with their hips. Some versions allowed forearms or rackets.

facts.hook: Ice hockey debuted at a Summer Olympics, held in April 1920
facts.body: The tournament was played at Antwerp's Ice Palace in April, as an early start to the Games.

facts.hook: India began a run of six straight Olympic field hockey golds in 1928
facts.body: At Amsterdam 1928 India won its first Olympic gold in field hockey. It was the first of six in a row.

facts.hook: In 1896 Olympic swimming took place in the open sea, in cold water
facts.body: The organizers wouldn't pay for a special venue, so the races were swum in open sea, in a cold bay where the swimmers suffered.

facts.hook: An unknown water carrier won the first Olympic marathon and became a national hero
facts.body: At Athens 1896 Spyridon Louis, who carried water for a living, won the marathon. He was the only Greek athletics champion at those Games.

facts.hook: The Olympic torch relay isn't ancient: it was first run for Berlin 1936
facts.body: It was the first time a flame from Olympia, in Greece, was carried to the host city by relay. It was promoted by Carl Diem of the organising committee.

facts.hook: Dorando Pietri was disqualified from the 1908 marathon after being helped to the finish
facts.body: He entered the stadium, took the wrong path and fell. Because he was helped by the umpires, he was disqualified, but Queen Alexandra awarded him a cup.

facts.hook: A Mexican woman was the first woman to light the Olympic cauldron, in 1968
facts.body: Enriqueta Basilio lit the cauldron at the opening ceremony of Mexico 1968, the first Games held in Latin America.

facts.hook: Bob Beamon's 1968 long jump stood as the world record for over twenty years
facts.body: Beamon leapt 8.90 m at Mexico 1968 for a world record. That mark lasted until 1991.

facts.hook: At Paris 1900, Spain won Olympic Basque pelota without playing: the rivals withdrew
facts.body: Only two teams entered, France and Spain. The French pair withdrew on the afternoon of the contest, so the Spanish pair, Amezola and Villota, were awarded the gold medal.

facts.hook: Olympic gold, silver and bronze began at the 1904 Games
facts.body: It was at St. Louis in 1904 that the Games first awarded gold, silver and bronze to the top three in each event.

facts.hook: El Santo, a lucha libre legend, was buried wearing his silver mask
facts.body: He kept wearing the mask after retiring and showed his face only briefly in old age. For luchadores, the mask is synonymous with their identity.

facts.hook: The marathon's 42.195 km was fixed in 1921, copying the 1908 London Games
facts.body: The 1908 course ran from Windsor Castle to the White City Stadium in London. The IAAF set that length as the standard marathon distance in May 1921.

facts.hook: Pelota mixteca is played with gloves that can weigh 3 to 6 kg
facts.body: It is a game with roots centuries old, perhaps millennia, still played in Oaxaca and Guerrero. Players strike the ball with large gloves that can weigh 3 to 6 kg.

facts.hook: A sumo wrestler can face an opponent up to twice his own weight
facts.body: Professional sumo has no weight divisions. With superior technique, smaller wrestlers can control and defeat much larger opponents.

facts.hook: According to ancient paintings, sumo began as a ritual dance praying for a good harvest
facts.body: The first mention of sumo, in the Kojiki manuscript of 712, says that two kami (gods) settled in a wrestling match who owned the Japanese islands.

facts.hook: “Ping-pong” imitates the sound of the game and became a registered trademark
facts.body: The name imitates the sound of the game. The manufacturer J. Jaques & Son registered it as a trademark.

facts.hook: The Tour de France was created to boost a newspaper's sales
facts.body: Journalist Géo Lefèvre suggested a race all around France, and the newspaper L'Auto first organized it in 1903 to increase its sales.

facts.hook: The 1904 Tour de France disqualified its leading riders, the winner included
facts.body: Cheating was rife in the 1904 race. In the end the leading riders, including the winner Maurice Garin, were disqualified.

facts.hook: Volleyball was born in 1895 as a gentler alternative to basketball
facts.body: William G. Morgan, a YMCA director in Holyoke, devised it as a less physically demanding alternative to basketball. He first called it "mintonette".

facts.hook: Hangul's consonants are thought to depict the speech organs
facts.body: Five basic consonants are based on the shapes of human speech organs, and most of the others add lines to those letters. Other inspirations for the shapes have been proposed but remain debated.

facts.hook: Pirahã, an Amazonian language, can be whistled, hummed or turned into music
facts.body: This language of a people in Amazonas, Brazil, is not only spoken: it can also be whistled, hummed or encoded in music.

facts.hook: In Pirahã, the words once taken for "one" and "two" seem to mean "few" and "more"
facts.body: They were first described as "one" and "two", but Everett later said they mean "small quantity" and "larger quantity", and experiments found them more likely to be relative terms. The language lacks exact quantity words.

facts.hook: Silbo Gomero, whistled Spanish, can carry messages up to five kilometres
facts.body: This system from La Gomera, in the Canary Islands, turns spoken Spanish into whistling. It has been used to communicate across the island's deep ravines and narrow valleys.

facts.hook: The letter ñ began as an abbreviation: a tilde over an n stood for two n's
facts.body: Medieval writers shortened the Latin double n by writing a single n with a wavy line above it. That mark became the tilde of the Spanish ñ.

facts.hook: The English word "canyon" is the adapted form of the Spanish "cañón"
facts.body: When cañón entered English it lost its tilde and became canyon. Other Spanish words, like jalapeño, piñata or El Niño, keep the ñ.

facts.hook: A Greek palindrome meaning "wash my sins, not only my face" was carved on fonts
facts.body: The phrase "nipson anomemata me monan opsin" is attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus, from the 4th century. Written in Greek letters it reads the same both ways, and it was inscribed on fonts in many churches.

facts.hook: "Saippuakivikauppias" ("soapstone vendor") is among the longest palindromic words
facts.body: This 19-letter Finnish word reads the same backwards. Guinness World Records lists it as the longest palindromic word in everyday use.

facts.hook: "Esperanto" was its creator's pen name; the language was "the international language"
facts.body: Ophthalmologist L. L. Zamenhof published the first Esperanto grammar in 1887 under the pseudonym Doktoro Esperanto. He simply called the language la lingvo internacia, "the international language".

facts.hook: To build Morse code, Alfred Vail counted the movable type at a local newspaper
facts.body: Vail estimated how often each English letter is used by counting the type in the type cases of a local newspaper. The most common letters got the shortest sequences of dots and dashes.

facts.hook: Morse first planned to send only numbers and look words up in a codebook
facts.body: His earliest design transmitted numerals that were looked up in a codebook. Alfred Vail soon expanded the code, in 1840, to include letters and special characters.

facts.hook: Modern Icelanders can understand sagas written about 800 years ago
facts.body: Apart from new vocabulary, written Icelandic has not changed substantially since the 11th century. The sagas are usually read with modern spelling and footnotes, but are otherwise intact.

facts.hook: Icelandic prefers to coin its own words for new things rather than import them
facts.body: The language regulator actively coins terms from older Icelandic words rather than taking in loanwords, and the effort to create new words continues, especially for science and technology.

facts.hook: In Georgian, 93 is literally "four times twenty plus thirteen"
facts.body: Georgian counts in twenties, like Basque and, partly, French. Numbers between 20 and 100 are the largest multiple of 20 plus the remainder.

facts.hook: Maltese is the only Semitic language officially written in the Latin alphabet
facts.body: It descends from medieval Sicilian Arabic, yet it is written with Latin letters. It is also an official language of Malta and of the European Union.

facts.hook: Atatürk's 1927 speech had to be "translated" three times into modern Turkish
facts.body: He used the formal Ottoman style of his day. After the language reform it sounded so alien that the speech was "translated" in 1963, 1986 and 1995. Ironically, the body behind that reform was founded under his patronage.

facts.hook: Since 2007, Cyrillic has been the European Union's third official script
facts.body: It became the third when Bulgaria joined the EU in 2007. The other two official scripts are Latin and Greek.

facts.hook: The Phoenician alphabet had 22 letters, and all of them were consonants
facts.body: It did not write vowels, though late varieties sometimes marked a few. The Greek alphabet derives from it, and the Greeks added the vowels to the consonant-only Phoenician letters.

facts.hook: Phoenician's simple alphabet allowed common people to learn how to write
facts.body: Each sound had one symbol, so there were only a few dozen signs to learn. Cuneiform and hieroglyphs used many complex characters and had restricted literacy to a small elite.

facts.hook: Chinese characters reached Japan on objects such as a gold seal from the year 57
facts.body: A well-known early example is the King of Na gold seal, given by Han emperor Guangwu to an emissary from Japan. Widespread writing in Japan developed later, especially from the fifth century onward.

facts.hook: A silversmith who never learned English invented the Cherokee syllabary
facts.body: Sequoyah, who never went to school, began around 1809 and by 1821 had 86 symbols, later streamlined to 85, one per syllable. The Cherokee Nation officially adopted it in 1825.

facts.hook: Sequoyah used his daughter to prove that his writing system worked
facts.body: His daughter Ayokeh was the first person to learn it. To show its value, he had local leaders say words aloud, wrote them down, and called her in to read them back.

facts.hook: Rotokas, from Bougainville Island, is written with just 12 letters
facts.body: Its Latin alphabet has a, e, g, i, k, o, p, r, s, t, u and v, with no diacritics, and long vowels are written doubled. It is spoken on Bougainville Island, in Papua New Guinea.

facts.hook: "Quarantine" had a 30-day predecessor, the "trentino", imposed in Ragusa in 1377
facts.body: Quarantine comes from quarantena, "forty days". It followed the trentino, a 30-day isolation first imposed in 1377 in the Republic of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik in Croatia.

facts.hook: "Volapük" means "language of the world" and comes from English "world" and "speak"
facts.body: Johann Martin Schleyer, a German priest, created this constructed language in 1879. Its name joins vol and pük, taken from English, with a genitive ending.

facts.hook: The name "toki pona" mixes a word from Tok Pisin and one from Esperanto
facts.body: It means "the language of good" or "simple language". Toki comes from Tok Pisin tok, itself from English talk; pona, from Esperanto bona.

facts.hook: Toki Pona gets by on about 120 words: "friend" is "good person"
facts.body: Canadian Sonja Lang published early drafts of this invented language online in 2001. Her 2014 book presents around 120 words, combined for complex ideas: jan pona, "good person", can mean friend.

facts.hook: A novel without the letter e, "La Disparition", was translated into Spanish without the a
facts.body: Georges Perec wrote La Disparition without using the letter e. The Spanish translation instead leaves out the letter a.

facts.hook: The earliest known lipogram author, in the 6th century BCE, avoided the letter sigma
facts.body: Lasus of Hermione left sigma out of an Ode to the Centaurs and a Hymn to Demeter. Only the first verse of the hymn survives.

facts.hook: The earliest known printed "O.K." appeared on 23 March 1839, in Boston
facts.body: It ran in the Boston Morning Post, in a line widely credited to editor Charles Gordon Greene.

facts.hook: Until 1979, Star Trek's Klingons always spoke English
facts.body: Actor James Doohan devised the basic sounds and a few words for the first film in 1979. Marc Okrand later developed Klingon into a full-fledged language.

facts.hook: Hamlet and the Epic of Gilgamesh have been published in Klingon
facts.body: So has Much Ado About Nothing. The Shakespeare picks were inspired by Chancellor Gorkon in Star Trek VI, who says you have not experienced Shakespeare until you read him "in the original Klingon".
